It is no flattery, but an uncontested truth to aver, that you have been most eminently useful to this kingdom, in encouraging the fine arts and manufactures. The extensive share of literature and discerning judgment you enjoy, would not permit the curious monuments of Irish antiquity to pass unnoticed ; at your own private expence very able artists have been employed to make such a Collection of Drawings of these Monuments as give infinite pleasure to every lover of antiquity to behold. Permit me, Sir, to join the public voice, in hoping, that

### OF THE
# LITERATURE
### OF THE
# IRISH NATION
### IN
## HEATHENISH TIMES.

Amongst all the proofs that can be exhibited of the existence of letters and learning in pagan times, no one can be so much depended on, as the producing of certain works, that were really written by pagan authors, and which existed before St. Patrick’s arrival in this island : Such a proof would doubtless solve the question proposed, in a decisive manner. The *dans* or poems given us by Keating to attest the histories of remote times, far from assisting us on the occasion, rather have appeared to many as proofs against us, because the words, the style, and the very poetic dress of these poems, show them to be of modern date and invention. Most of that historian’s poetic quotations regarding the *Belgian* and *Danian* colonies, the *lia fail*, &c. are taken from poems that, by the *book of Lecan*, are attri-

uncouth dress, must become disagreeable to the modern reader, who sought for elegancy of style, plain language and pleasure in his reading. And hence, as it would be highly contradictory to all good reason, for a man to conclude, that a fact or revolution, happening in any of the aforesaid great empires, had for its only authority an Irish Christian poet, because such a fact or revolution was really described by him, so in like manner it is repugnant to good sense, that a Christian poet should be assigned as the only author for facts which happened in heathenish times, because these facts are recorded in his verses; the reason he records in his poetry the facts relating to those empires of the world, is, because he read the history of them, and understood the language wherein the facts were contained, and by a like reason doth he record in verse, the facts regarding his own country, because he is well acquainted with the history of it, and understands his native language to perfection.

In my humble opinion the verses of such poets deserve the greatest credit, since they lay before us the most absurd relations and ridiculous tenets of our pagan ancestors, as well as the most certain and well connected points of their doctrine and history. This could not proceed from a want of discernment and good sense in them, since they show by other writings, they were well acquainted with foreign history, poetry and oratory, and consequently had as good a right as we have to distinguish between palpable error and truth, or plausibility; and since they relate these palpable errors and fabulous story, it appears, their true motive

for so doing was to hand down these accounts,

rives one advantage from their fidelity viz. that
we can by that means take a retrograde view of
pagan blindness and misery.
   Having thus offered my thoughts in vindication
of these verses, which I suppose to have been com-
posed by Christian poets, celebrated in their times,
(for I know what little dependance ought to be had
on the versification of our modern bards) I shall
now proceed to give some clear proofs of our
having had the use of letters before Christianity.
The proof I speak of is the exhibition of a frag-
ment of a Code of Laws, which, I think, every ju-
dicious reader, who is versed in Irish antiquities,
will judge to have been the product of very remote
times, much higher than the fifth or sixth centuries.
   This fragment contains twelve folios, and begins
at folio sixty-four, the sixty-three preceding were
missing ; and here I must beg the reader to remark,
the difference between the letter of the law and the
explication of the said law. I maintain the first is of
pagan institution, and that the second is the work
of one or many Christian Jurisconsults, who inter-
preted this law, and applied it to particular cases,
according to the intention of the Christian legislator.
   This collection was partly made in the time of
Donal mac Aoda mac Anmirech, who was a Christian
prince, by Ceandfaela mac Aillil, called I suppose
*Ceandfaela na fogluma* ; and partly by Aicill who
lived after Ceandfaela’s time, (on the environs of
Tara) and after the time of king Cormac, for he

<meta>catchword: Plebiscita</meta>

was cotemporary with *Carbre Liffeachair* son of *Cormac*. Nevertheless the work is attributed to *Cormac*, as it was begun by him and ended in the reign of his son *Carbre*; so that the Irish lawyers who compiled and delivered this code of laws, were *Aicill* who lived in the reigns of *Cormac* and of his son *Carbre*, and *Ceandfaela* son of *Aillil*, who flourished in the reign of *Donal* son of *Hugh mac Ainmirech*. No doubt but that these laws were collected by the order of those Irish princes, just as we know the Roman emperor *Justinian I.* who had the Roman laws collected, by the care and labour of ten able Jurisconsults, directed in chief by the celebrated *Trebonianus*, calling this collection the *Justinian Code*; he also caused the scattered decisions of his judges and magistrates, reduced to the number of fifty, to be called *digesta* or *pandectæ*, to all which he added his four books of institutes, which are an abridgment of the text of all the Roman laws; and lastly he published his own laws which he called *novellæ*; this compilation has procured for that emperor an immortal name.

Our Irish Christian legislators took the same method with the Christian Jurisconsult *Trebonianus* and his illustrious assistants called *antecessores* or professors and interpreters, for in the preface to the *Pandectæ*, they are stiled των νόμων διδασκάλοις, I mean *Theophilus* and *Dorotheus*, who explained not only the laws of the Christian emperors from the year 527, when *Justinian* succeeded his uncle *Justin* in the empire, up to the reign of *Constantine the Great*, but also to the times of *Julius* and *Augustus Cæsar*. They even introduce the laws of the senate and the

It is then related of him that he was educated at Tuam Dercain, at the meeting of three roads, centrical to the houses of three suad or virtuosi, viz. a genealogist, a poet, and a sai leigind; his capacity and memory are praised, and concludes, that whatever he learned by day from his three teachers, he carefully wrote down at night in *cailc liubar*, a chalk book.

According to Tigernach, Cinfaela, stiled by him *sapiens*, died in the year 679.

Then follows concerning Cormac and Carbre Liffeachair his son, and the history of Cormac's being blinded is mentioned thus:

Ceallach son of Cormac ravished a Lagenian lady of quality, daughter to Solar son of Artcorb, in her father's house at Rath Aedha in Leinster; some time after Aongus Gaibuaibnech passing through Connaught, went into the house of a woman of the free state of Luigne, and forcibly drank milk there *ro cait bainde in ar eigin*; upon which she told him, he had better revenge himself on Ceallach for violating his brother Solar's honour, than infringe on the liberty of that state; which reproach made so deep an impression on the mind of Aongus, that he immediately went home, put on his armour, and after the setting of the sun, met Cormac and his son Ceallach, when at one blow he put Ceallach to death, and with his armed elbow struck Cormac blind; but the famous Aicil performed a cure for his eye.

It is then related that Cormac's part of this book is *arafefer & na blai*, but that Cinfaela's part is the rest of the book.

It is then mentioned that the Latin *suum licet* is in Irish called *deimin dilmain*; that its indirect signification is called by him *buna airs*; that *coitchen* means common, *diles* proper, and *ruidles* entire, safe and sound; that there are eight common terms of the laws called *ocht nernaille coitchena*, viz.

->INETG or FOGARCAILE,<-
->LANFRAC or COMRAILE,<-

->AITHGIN or IN IMDEITHBIR,<-
->TORBA,<-
->SLAN,<-

->FODLAIDETU.<-

The rest of this folio is effaced.

The next page begins a kind of exordium to the work thus, *aslach on athair for Ebha & toltnugad do Ebba fria*, i. e. the serpent presented the forbidden fruit to Eve, and Eve consented to receive it. *Imarbas*, is the prohibition of a legislator. *Com fugud do Adam fria flatarta um coimde*, i. e. Eve delivered it to Adam in disobedience to the Trinity; and hence it is plain, says the author, that when a man knows a crime in virtue of the law established, though he be ignorant of the penalty enjoined by it, he may be punished according to the full measure; is as sin is follos o bias fis in cinaid ac duine gen coraib fis na berce con adhainfis lanfrach, and hence by a greater right, when the crime or fault is known and the penalty too, there is no matter for deception, *ni damna meallaid*.

and all anger is *Elguin*; for a man doth many things through *Elguin* which are not of anger, and does nothing through anger which is not of *Elguin*, therefore *Elguin* is a more extensive term than anger or *ferg* (b). *Ni can elguin is ferg is gach ferg is elguin; do gena duine moran tre elguin nad bi ferg, agus ni digne tri ferg ni na bi helguin; is fairleithe elguin ina ferg defide.* ●

**Anfot for Espa. I. fuirre foi Esba Anfot,** i. e. *anfot* is greater than or over *espa*, or *anfot* is inferior to *esba*. The word *fuirre* is the comparative degree of *fa* or *fo* under, and corresponds with the Latin word *inferius* from *infra*, and means here less extensive in its signification and import, or applicable to fewer principles and cases. The kind of argument above mentioned is also used thus: every *espa* is *anfot*, but every *anfot* is not *espa*; for a man performs many actions through *anfot* which are not *espa*, therefore *anfot* is more extensive than *esba*.

**Toiscide for Torba**, Toiscide is more extensive than Torba, and the same kind of reasoning is made use of. N. B. Toiscide is the will, desire, or inclination. Ni can toiscide is torba, & gach torba is toiscide; uair do genead duine moran tria toiscide na bi torba, agus ni digne tria torba na bi toiscide; is forleite toiscide desin ina torba.

---

(b) This reasoning is a true philosophical argument of an antecedent and consequent, called in philosophy *Enthymema* the antecedent whereof is clearly demonstrated. This distinction between the terms, together with the many others equally discernible in this fragment, proves that the Irish legislator was accurately versed in the philosophy of the great Aristotle, according to whom such terms are styled *termini magis et minus communes.*

**NO FRITHAIG TORBA. i: FIR INDSAIGE DO IN BAILE IMBITH AG DENAM GNIM TORB;** means one who assists a second person to commit a crime against law, and such a person is to make satisfaction in the one-third of the damage and penalty; *a dilfe do conuice a trian*; the same is to hold good if having it in his power to hinder the principal aggressor's escape when condemned or judgment passed, and he does not hinder it; some think it only means a person who without any assistant infringes the law. In a marginal note it is mentioned, that *fritaig* signifies any single man who commits a crime against the law, having another person to countenance and support him therein; to which it is added, that if the first person be acquitted and obliged to pay no <term>eric</term> or pecuniary fine, the *fir indsaige* or assistant will thereby be also exempted from paying one-third.

**TEORA FODLA FOGLA.** <term>Fogla</term> is three-fold, viz. by *gne cinel cinelach & subalter*; by *cinel* is meant species, and by *gne* genus; there is a *gne* in *comraite*, in *tafot*, in *torba*, and in *teasba*, but they are all species deriving under *etguin*, which is more extensive than any of them, and the genus of all: *ag aitfeagad don etguin*; nevertheless it derives itself under the four *fogla*, and these again derive under the twelve divisions of *etguin*, so that the genus is under its genus as a subalternum.

**BRA**, means the judge or <term>breheaman</term>.

**CID DECHRUITHE**, is a term signifying, where is the criminal?

proceed from the place being so called after the person.

Here ends the Fragment, so that all the rest of the blai are wanting, and all that part composed by Cinfaela and promulgated by Donal mac Aeda mac Aimirech king of Ulster.

The impartial reader, after perusing this extract, will easily see that my distinction between the text of the law, and the explication of the text, is well grounded; that the former is of a much higher antiquity than the Christian era, though the latter was really the composition of a Christian. The style of the text is extremely ancient, and the language admitted of many expositions, even from a writer whose time seems to approach within a century or two at the most of St. Patrick’s. He sometimes gives many and opposite senses to the same term, and at other times cites the authority of the ancients in order to explain himself. In a word, every character discernible in the text, demonstrates its antiquity, and proves it is truly and genuinely the work of the Pagan Juris-consult and of the Pagan Irish princes to whom it is attributed; which being duly proved, most positively evinces the use of letters at least long before the epoch of Christianity in this island.

I do not recollect to have met any where with the words *cailc luibar*, a chalk book; it seems to denote that Cormac used tablets, covered with some certain kind of matter, fit to smooth the surfaces, and to render them fit to inscribe, what he thought proper on them. The word *cailc* indeed means *chalk*, but it may also denote parchment rendered white by chalk. The true sense requires to be cleared up by other passages in our Irish monuments, and for this reason I leave it to the better

Now as the laws regarding manſlaughter form the firſt part of the ſection called *na blai*, and that the explication of the terms ſerved only for a preparation to that part, I ſhall take notice of ſome curious and uſeful circumſtances tending to illuſtrate thoſe laws. The *Eric* or fine for manſlaughter ſpecified in the above fragment, did not regard the perſon who committed the fact, but was payable to the provincial king, from the *petty ſtate* or principality wherein the body of a man or woman was found dead, unleſs the chief of that ſtate had the particular privilege and faculty of having his people exempted from ſuch a fine; which indeed was one of the moſt conſiderable immunities a provincial king could beſtow on a chief of his province. There was a difference obſerved in the infliction of this fine, for if the fact was proved to be wilful murder, the fine was rigorous, if involuntary, it was leſs rigorous, and in both caſes proportioned to the dignity or baſeneſs of the deceaſed perſon’s condition. And although the aggreſſor did ſuffer the penalty which the law inflicted, the diſtrict or ſtate whererein the crime was perpetrated, was not thereby exempted in the leaſt degree from paying the fine. This rigour obliged the natives of any diſtrict to be careful and vigilant in preſerving each others lives, as well as of ſtrangers, leſt they ſhould ſuffer through the malice and wickedneſs of others. And certain it is, that many misfortunes which we ſee happen daily amongſt us, may be efficaciouſly prevented by ſuch means; the natives of a diſtrict having it often in their power to obviate them. was for that reason, without doubt, our Irish legislators enacted such laws: I do not remember to have seen any example of the kind of punishment, which these laws inflicted on a man guilty of murder; they all regarded the state or region wherein the facts were committed; except one in the *Liber Lecanus*, where it is mentioned a person was fined seven *cumalas* (twenty-one cows) for having wounded an ecclesiastic in the arm; and I have read, that the ancestor of *O'Mora*, lord of the country, now called Queen's county, by a special grace, had his state exempted from paying *Eric* or fine, to the king of Leinster, in case of murder or manslaughter happening in any part thereof.

We must observe that the Irish fines are mostly specified by paying *cumalas*, which word according to its modern acceptance, since the Christian era, means only three cows; but I have somewhere met with that expression regarding Pagan times, wherein it denoted men or women slaves, guilty of crimes deserving death, which were delivered up as a part of the *Eric*, to be sacrificed to the manes of the deceased.

natives, and from the political circumstances in

their neighbours, as well as from their own com-

According to the tenure of our Iriſh laws, all females were excluded from having any ſhare in the chief adminiſtration of affairs, as well with regard to the government of the whole kingdom, as to its petty ſtates and inferior principalities; for no other reaſon, without doubt, than that theſe ſtates required military ſervice, for which the female ſex was diſqualified by nature. In effect they found themſelves ſituated among different tribes of people, whose principal repreſentatives were ſometimes ambitious, and unjuſt enough to encroach on their landed properties; the falſe glory of being eſteemed more powerful and more expert in war than their neighbours, joined to their intereſts and the advancement of their reſpective trials, often determined theſe men to diſturb the public quiet, and endeavour to raiſe themſelves on the ruins of others. Hence followed a political neceſſity in every branch or ſept, to chuſe out for their chief and leaders, men of known valour and experience, to fight their battles ſucceſſively, and to defend their landed properties againſt all invaders. And hence the maxims of excluding women from inheriting landed properties was as ſacred amongſt the ancient Iriſh, as amongſt the Franks, or any other people. And as the lands of all the petty ſtates did abſolutely and indiſpenſably exclude women from inheriting them, ſo the ſame law gradually became general, and deſcended to the loweſt denomination of land proprietors.

The above Iriſh ſpecimen deſcribes the injustice of alienating the lands from the male line, in favour of women, by the expreſſive term of **TIR DO BEIR DAR BRAIGIT FINE.** At this day when a man encroaches on any lands, and takes it to farm, by underhand dealing and unknown terms, *do ghlac ſe tar mo braigid è*, or elſe, as *gniomh fill do rin ſe mo thalamb do ghlaca thar mo bhraghaid amach*; by which it would appear, that when the male line of one family was extinct, the estate was to devolve on the ſept or *fine*, and became the property of their males.

The ſame law was obſerved by other European nations; the Goths and Vandals excluded women from ſucceeding to the throne. We have a very remarkable inſtance of this, in the hiſtory of *Amalaſuntha*, daughter to the famous *Theodoric*, (and mother of *Athelric*) king of the *Oſtrogoths*. This princeſs, whoſe bright genius and eminent knowledge of the Greek and Latin tongues will always do her memory honour, was nevertheleſs diſqualified to reign after the death of her ſon, on account of her ſex, and married *Theodatus*, with a view to exerciſe all regal power under his name, in which however ſhe found herſelf fatally miſtaken in 534. See *Caſſiodor. var. lib. 10.*

The Irish in primitive times were not only at-

favour of the male line, from a political and neces-

justice, in sharing equitably with the males of
their respective families. They shewed particular
honour to their chiefs, and these in return did not
despise their inferiors, in the distribution of goods.
The heads of families considered that the support
of their friends and relations in time of war,
was absolutely necessary, both for repelling the
power of their enemies and advancing their mili-
tary conquests and therefore they judged that the
sanction of rewards and a fair and honest partition
of landed properties, which were often the fruit
of their common valour, was the most firm and
efficacious cement of union, that could subsist
between the prince and his relations. Hence the
very nature of these military tenures rendered them
capable of being divided and subdivided between
the males of the first proprietors, and hence the
law of gavelling them took its rise, and was as
universally observed in this kingdom, as the very
law of excluding the female sex from any share in
them, has been proved to be...

This gavelling ſettlement the Iriſh called GABHALTUS CINE, or GABHAIL CINE, literally meaning FAMILY-SETTLEMENT; from whence the Engliſh formed the term GAVEL-KIND. GABHALTUS or GABHAIL, pronounced GAVAIL, in Iriſh ſignifies any landed ſettlement, lately acquired by conqueſt, by inheritance, or by contract; but its etymologycal meaning is CONQUEST. Thus by the words LEABHAR NA GABHALA is underſtood the book of Conqueſts; and in the Iriſh hiſtory of Thomond called *Caithreim Toirdealbhaig*, deſcribing the bloody wars carried on between the O'Briens of Thomond and thoſe of Arra, in the thirteenth century, the ſettlement or eſtate which the latter poſſeſſed themſelves of in the country of Arra, is called GABHALTUS.

The Franks obſerved the ſame law of dividing the tenures called Salic lands. Abbe Du Bos ſhows a remarkable inſtance of that truth; he quotes for his voucher the celebrated Bodinus, citing the teſtamentary act of a gentleman of Guyenne, whereby the father divides between his ſons, the Salic or feodal lands of which he was proprietor. And in the ſame place, this author obſerves, that in all appearance thoſe military benefices were the true origin of the landed properties called FIEFS NOBLE, or tenures in military ſervice.

The Anglo-Saxons alſo obſerved this cuſtom; it is well known they divided their landed intereſts between the poſſeſſor's children, which they called in their language GIFE-AL-KIN, a word nearly ſimilar in ſound and in meaning to the Iriſh term GABHAIL-CINE.

The Welsh, who are the remains of the old Britons, in like manner observed this law, at all times, exactly in the same manner as the Irish, and continued so to do until the thirty-second year of Henry the Eighth's reign. See War. Antiq. Hib. c. 8. Davis Hist. relat. p. 20.

It is then no way surprising, that the chief STRONGBONIAN families, exclusive of those confined within the English pale about Dublin, observed the same old custom at their first settling in this kingdom. The FITZGERALDS, the BARRYS, the BURKS, &c. &c. were as observant of it as the Irish; and whether they derived it from the practice of their ancestors the FRANCO-NORMANS and Welsh, who religiously observed it, as I have shown, or whether they conformed themselves to it, as they did to the other customary laws of this nation, certain it is, that they did strictly follow it. Upon all these different specimens of Irish Gavels, several observations do naturally occur. First, that either the fathers or the seniors of families generally observed an equitable and sometimes an equal portion of shares, between the males of the said families, whereof we see perfect examples in the preceding gavels. Secondly, that the *natural sons* had their equal shares, as well as the sons born in lawful wedlock; from both which circumstances, we have reason to conclude, that this custom was grounded on the patriarchal or primitive law of nature, and consequently derived from a principle of a more ancient establishment than the laws of Christian princes, whereby *bastards* are excluded from succeeding to the family estate, while the legitimate children are living. Thus according to the same primitive law, Jacob’s sons by the handmaids of his wives Leah and Rachel, are ranked amongst the *heads of the twelve tribes of Israel*, upon a level in

It is also remarkable, that it was generally the senior, and not the direct heir in lineal descent from the common stock, who was qualified to make this gavel, because he was the chief proprietor ; of this we see a clear instance in the Cuanagh gavel made by Conor mor O'Brien, whose cousin-german Turlogh son of Thady, surnamed Anchomraic (the fighter) was the direct heir, this Thady being the elder brother of Mortogh father to Conor mor. Notwithstanding we see that Conor, by his right of seniority, was chief of the family, proprietor of its landed estates, and solely qualified to make the gavel; the text runs thus : *Tug an Conchur morsa leath na codach ranna fearainn rainig e fein do dhibh mhac Taidg an chomhraic air a mbeith na sinfior braithrech aige* ; he explains this matter fully by the following words, *dob oge an Muirtheartach so athair Chonchubhair mhoir na Taidhg an chomhraic*.

Another observation, equally curious, may be noticed, viz. that though the chief or senior stints himself to a bare equality of share with every other male of the family, yet he reserves the chief property of the estate as vested in himself during his life, by subjecting all the other shares to a chief rent, which was to be paid him in an humble and dutiful manner. This was doubtless slight and inconsiderable, nevertheless it was a sufficient mark both of his authority over them, and of their dependency on him, as their chief lord ; in a word,

Hence what Strabo applies to the *Aſiatic Iberians* was equally applicable to the *Irifh nation* in former times. *Hi omnia per familias communia habent; ſed is imperat et rem habet qui ſenior eſt.*

Now as the reſerve of chief rent on the gavelled lands, not only eſtabliſhed the ſway, and influence of the chief lord, or head of the family, over all the members of the tribe, and likewise ſecured for him a reverſion of the eſtate when the actual tenants either forfeited or died without iſſue; ſo this cuſtom was not, and could not be then attended with any conſequences ſo deſtructive of the ſplendor of a family, as it muſt be in our days. In ancient times the dignity of a chief did not depend on pecuniary revenues; it conſiſted in his power and influence over the tribe he governed, in the affluence of proviſions he had for his houſhold, and in the number of fighting men he could command to vindicate his rights, to afſiſt his friends, or to enlarge his conqueſts. And as to the ſplendor of the tribe in general, it conſiſted in their numbers, in the full and peaceable enjoyment of their rights, and in their capacity of furniſhing their family chiefs with their different ſupplies.

In fine, the Gavel cuſtom, as it was obſerved by the ancient Irifh, appears to have been perfectly reconcileable with the exigencies of the ſtate, and with the dignity of any chieftain, were he even a

By the first, we are enabled to pass a right judgment on those ancient times; and thus when we find notions seriously delivered for truths, that are notoriously incompatible with the first principles of Christianity, and are known to be the tenets of pagan persuasion, then no reasonable cause of doubt remains for us to conclude, that such writ-ings are of pagan times.

The word **ANAK** which means a giant or hero, seems to be the radix of the Greek *anax*, genitive *anaktos*, the usual term for a king; the septuagint interpreters translate **MELECH** and **MELCHI**, a king, into *anax*, *anakta*, or *anacta*; this however was not its true and proper meaning, it first imported a saviour or defender, and as this was the true office of a sovereign, and the motive for creating him was to defend and protect a people or kindred from destruction or oppression, so it was not unnatural it should become the first appellative of a king. Homer calls Agamemnon and others by this name; Jupiter is stiled *anax* of gods and men; nevertheless the inferior gods are stiled *anaktes* to signify defenders or saviours. Asty-anax was a title the Trojans gave Scamandrius the son of Hector, which according to Homer’s interpretation, meant a defender of the city. See *Iliad*, vi. 399. Now the Irish word **ANAC** or **ANAIK**, means *save*, *defend*; thus we say *anaic sinn a Thiarna*, *save*, *protect us, O Lord*; *anacal* means protection, also the safe-guard of a prince, and *anac clan*, sometimes written *eneaclan*, is the term in the Brehon laws, for the tribute paid by the clan or tribe, to the chief, for his protection.

The obscure traditional accounts preserved in the old Irish manuscripts, and renewed by Keating and others, that the ancestors of the first inhabitants of Ireland, first settled in Crete and other islands of the Mediterranean sea, as also in Egypt, Greece, Spain, &c. do apparently point out to the reader, the state and progress of the *Phenicians*, after their expulsion under the conduct of Cadmus,

The Irish call the month of May *Bel-tine*, or fire of Belus, and the first day of May *la Bel-tine*, or the day of Belus’s fire; they call the eve of the first of November *oidche Shamhna* (corruptly pronounced ee owna) or the eve of Samen, which was the Carthaginian name of the Sun. Mr. Martin in his history of the western isles of Scotland, which were peopled by the ancient Irish, observes, they had a deity named Belus or Belinus, which seems to have been the Assyrian God Bel, and probably from this pagan deity comes the Scots term of *Beltin*, the first day of May, having its first rise from the custom practised by the druids in those isles, of extinguishing all the fires in the parish until the tythes were paid, and upon payment of them, the fires were kindled in each family, and never till then. In those days, continues the author, malefactors were burnt between two fires; hence, when they would express a man to be in a great straight, they say he is *between two fires of Bel*, which in their language they express thus, *edir dha thinne Bheal*, p. 105.

Some Mountains in Ulster still bear the name
of Bel-tine; but in the southern part of the king-
dom the name more frequently occurs. At the
foot of Knocmaoldown mountain, near Clogheen
in co. of Tipperary, is Logh Bheal or Belus’s Lake;
on the Moanmhullagh mountains, not far distant
from this lake, is Barn na Bheal a mullach, i. e. the
Gap of Belus on the summit; the usual salutation
of the common people was *Bel de dhuit*, the God
Belus to you; the meaning of which not being un-
derstood by the present race, they now say *Bal o*
*Dhia dhuit*, which they interpret thus, a mark from
God to you; bal signifying a spot or blemish, a
very improper term for a salutation; this is pecu-
liar to the counties of Waterford and Kilkenny.

The month of May was indeed the most proper
season of the year to acknowledge the beneficent
favours of Belus or the Sun; as the month of No-
vember was, to acknowledge their gratitude to
the same deity; because in May, that great planet
begins to beautify the face of the earth; to nourish
its decayed plants and vegetables, and to put life
and warmth into its animal beings; and in Novem-
ber the harvest and the vintage is gathered into
the barn. Hence of all created objects, that planet
deserved most to be noticed and loved by rational
sublunary beings, because its benign influence
produced them health of body, and an acceptable
prospect of nourishment. And hence it was, with-
out doubt, that almost every pagan nation adored
this beautiful planet as the parent of nature, under
different names and appellations; a religion, which
as Mr. Young observes in his *Revelation*, p. 35.

took its rise in Chaldea, was soon carried into
Egypt, and from thence to Greece; it spread itself
also to the most distant parts of the world, and
infected not only the eastern but the western
Scythians and Tartars, but the Mexicans too, for
the Spaniards found it there. (See Gage's new
Survey of the West Indies, ch. 12.) Even the
descendants of Shem, whose posterity preserved
the memory of the true God for a longer time
than those of Ham or Japhet, at length transferred
their homage to the Sun and Moon. (Photius ex
Ctesia. Q. Curt. l. 8. c. 9. Philost. l. 3. ch. 35.)
    The ancient practice of adoring the Sun by the
symbol of fire, was first introduced into the world
by *Nimrod*, otherwise called *Baal* or *Belus*, which
in the Hebrew, Syriac and Phenician, literally
meant lord, or master. Belus is justly considered
by the learned to be the first who withdrew a con-
siderable number of people, employed by him in
building Babylon, from the true worship of God
to the spurious adoration of the Sun by fire.
This idolatrous mode of worship soon overspread
the earth, the Chanaanites or Phenicians observed
it in the same manner with the pagan Irish. We
read in the fourth book of Kings, that they served
Baal, and religiously passed their sons and daughters
through his fire, in which they were imitated by
the idolatrous Israelites. We also read in the same
book, that Achar king of Israel is blamed for having
religiously passed his son through the sacred pagan
fire; and it may be inferred from the said passage
that many Israelitish kings provoked God, by the
same idolatrous practice.

The appellative of Nembrod given also to Belus, which according to Isidorus literally signifies tyrant (Nembrod tyrannum significat. Etym. l. 17.) can more naturally and more conformably to ancient mythology, be investigated and cleared up in the Irish language. It is a complex of *nem* heaven, and *brod* captivity, insomuch that both words joined together by way of attribute to Belus grandson of Cham, plainly signify captivator of heaven, or *Cæli captivator*, or *Cælorum expugnator*. The Greek and Latin poets who describe the war of the giants against the gods, use no stronger expression to paint the insolence of the former, than *Cælos expugnare volebant*. Homer in his first Iliad introduces Venus, who reminds Jupiter of her services, by having delivered him from his captivity and chains, through her influence on the giant Briareus. Besides this argument, it further appears from the joint authority of several learned commentators on the first book of Genesis, that Belus had not the epithet Nembrod or Nimbrod given him, until the time of his impious undertaking in building the tower, which brought down upon him and his accomplices the immediate vengeance of God, not only by the total demolishment of that edifice, but also by a multiplication of the first language into several dialects, that were all understood by the three sons of Noah. (*Isidor. loco supra citato.*) Now if we consider Belus after this injurious undertaking, and his seduction of so many thousand people into idolatry and rebellion against God, we will readily conclude, he was the only person living, that most

If the Phenicians came from Spain to Ireland, it is probable they first planted themselves in the southern parts of the island ; accordingly I find some plausible reasons to think their chief settlement must have been in a large district of the county of Cork, which comprehends the entire barony of Fermoy and the half barony of Condons. This district was anciently called *Magh-Feine*, literally meaning the plains of the Phenians, *Phænio-magus* ; the inhabitants were always called *Feara Maigh Feine*, afterwards the word *Pheine* was left out, as making the name too tedious, and only a part of the compound preserved by the moderns, who to this day call it *Feára-maigh*, in English *Fermoy*.

The *Liber Lecanus* calls the inhabitants *Fir Magh Feine* ; the author or compiler of the annals of *Innisfallen*, at the year of Christ 254, mentions that Fiacha Muillethan, provincial king of Munster, bestowed this country called *Magh-Feine* to the celebrated druid Mogruth ; but the author of the Ulster book, in the *Liber Lecanus*, is more exact ; he mentions that in consideration of this druid's advice and influence over Cormac son of Con of the hundred battles, to give hostages to Fiacha Muillethan, after Cormac's signal defeat at the battle of Dun Claire, the Momonian prince gave him and his posterity for ever, the lands called *Magh mac Neirce*, which was afterwards called *Dal-Mog-ruith*, and formed only a part of *Magh-Feine*; It runs thus in verse :

The ingenious and learned antiquary, governor Pownal, has favoured us with an accurate drawing and description of another Phenician monument or sepulchral taphos, at New-Grange, near Drogheda, and of the Phenician inscription on one of the stones. See Archæolog. Soc. Antiq. Lond. vol. 2.

If the Tyrian Hercules, or any of the principal descendants of the Phenician colony he brought with him to Spain and the European isles, were leaders of the first people that inhabited this island; the solemn worship and sacrifices performed by them, may have been very agreeable to the pure patriarchal religion. And as Tyre, whereof Hercules was founder according to Herodotus, is mentioned in scripture as a well fortified city in Joshua’s time; and it seems also probable, that all the Chanaanites had not as yet fallen into idolatry, but that many of them still worshipped the true God; so we may conclude, that Hercules may possibly have been a worshipper of the true God, as well as Abimelech king of Gerar and his subjects, who were also Chanaaneans or Phenicians. # AN ESSAY

## IRISH ANTIQUITIES.

NATIONAL antiquities have always engaged the attention of every learned and polished people.  The inquiries of (a) Psammitichus into the original language, whatever truth may be in the anecdote, shows that such disquisitions were not unusual in former times, nor in the flourishing periods of antient empires.

Questions involving national honour naturally raise the flame of patriotism in every breast, and produce contests between kingdoms concerning their antiquities.  Intemperate zeal led to the fabrication of fictitious annals, and the wild (b) delusions of romantic history.  These excesses created a

<header>IRISH ANTIQUITIES.</header>

that antiquities, with every useful and ornamental branch of knowledge, received regal patronage. It was in the reign of king George II. that the society of antiquaries of London was incorporated.

To the animated exertions of individuals, and the munificent protection of a few noblemen and gentlemen, is England indebted for that great body of antient records and documents to be found in the British museum, and in the other public and private libraries of that kingdom. Unfortunately for Ireland, the same service was not rendered to her by any of her sons, except in a partial degree. A prey to the merciless ravages of the Ostmen; plundered by the (*f*) English adventurers; convulsed and torn by domestic broils; she shared every vicissitude of human misery, and preserved small remains of that piety and learning which made her the mart of literature and the admiration of Europe in the eighth and ninth centuries.

To retain the natives in their faith, the ecclesiastics, of the Romish profession, collected and published the lives of their (*g*) saints and collateral historical pieces. In these, and in the subsequent defence of them, many points of national antiquities were discussed and ascertained. Manuscripts were searched for and carefully examined, copies of them multiplied, and a foundation was laid for the

## BREHON LAWS.

Barred from every intercourse with the natives by the moſt penal ſtatutes, the Engliſh knew but little of their juriſprudence and municipal regulations ; every mention of their laws is, conſequently, in terms of deteſtation. As forfeitures were no part of the Brehonic inſtitutes, the Engliſh, who were conſtantly enriching themſelves by the delinquencies of the natives, without doubt, reprobated a ſyſtem ſo unfavourable to their ſchemes, and without minutely examining, pronounced it a lewd cuſtom.

### DRUIDIC LITERATURE.

Mr. Whitaker, who has written admirably on many parts of British Antiquities, studiously omits treating of the Druids, or their learning. That he considered it a barren or exhausted subject, the following brief observations sufficiently evidence.

<margin>(m) History of Manchester, book i. chap. 10. pag. 371, 372. of the edition in quarto.</margin>

> “All the various combinations, says (m) he, of the Noachidæ at Babel must have carried a regular alphabet away with them, to the places of their various dispersions. This most of them afterwards forgot. The Gauls in particular, had assuredly lost the use of their original alphabet, and in the days of Cæsar had adopted the Grecian from the neighbouring Greeks of Marseilles. The Britons also had forgot the knowledge of their original characters, and in the days of Tiberius had borrowed the Roman alphabet from the neighbouring Romans of Gaul. We find the most northerly states of Caledonia, a little after the victories of Vespasian and the conquests of Agricola, possest of an alphabet, and the celebrated Ossian, in the third century, making use of the Roman characters for his poems. # MODES OF INTERMENT.

The various modes of ſepulture practiſed by our anceſtors form a pleaſing and extenſive department in our antiquities. Sir James Ware has (a) treated it ſuperficially; but (b) Mr. Harris, with indefatigable induſtry, has made many valuable additions. The following remarks are given to excite attention, and as a ſpecimen of what hereafter may be executed on a larger ſcale.

**First Epoch.** Wormius has made a triple diviſion of the modes of interment; it is certainly not accurate, but whatever contributes to throw a confuſed ſubject into order has its uſe, and muſt elucidate it. Cremation he ſpeaks of firſt. Burning the body after death was univerſally prevalent in Europe in the earlieſt ages. It was (c) confefſedly ſo in Ireland. There is a very conciſe, but objectionable, manner of accounting for this and other oriental cuſtoms, by ſaying, they were introduced by Phenician colonies or Carthaginian traders. We can, in the preſent inſtance, recur to other and more ſatiſfactory evidence.

Odin, the great legiſlator and deity of the northern nations, arrived in Europe, with his Asiatic Goths, (d) twenty-four years before the chriſtian era;

**Second Epoch.** This Wormius calls the age of hillocks; when grandeur and more laboured sepulchres were formed, of considerable (k) height and surrounded with rows of stones. If the laws of Odin were observed, the practices of the first and second epochas were the same. Wormius grounds the distinction on the bodies being consigned to the earth whole in the latter, which had it been regular, made a material difference; but skeletons and urns full of burnt bones are frequently found in the same cemetery, which proves the impossibility of defining the duration of a custom, when it is fluctuating and about to give way to a new one. The time when burning was exchanged for burying in Ireland, was, according to our historians, in the reign of Eochadh, fourteen years before Christ. There is reason to believe, cremation was not disused for many years after, as Pomponius Mela, who lived in the first century of Christianity, tell us the Druids used both modes of interment. So that probably not before the full establishment of the Christian religion in this isle did cremation intirely cease. It was again revived during the domination of the Ostmen here, in the ninth and tenth centuries, who were then pagans. On account of this last circumstance, it is no easy matter to ascertain the date of those monuments.

Wormius, Mr. Pennant, the Compte de Caylus, and every other intelligent writer, allow these stone circles to be sepulchral; and that they certainly are sepulchral appears from a human body being found under each upright stone, in some circles lately opened in Connaught. So that after all that has been written on Stonehenge, it may be the sepulture of Hengist and the Anglo-Saxon chiefs; the first being buried under the altar, and the others under the trilithons.

These stone circles thus dedicated to religious uses, their application to other solemn purposes easily followed. Here kings were elected and inaugurated, and courts of justice and single combats were held. We had formerly in our (*q*) churches, plays, feasts, courts-leet and musters, and at present our kings are anointed there, all remains of ancient usages. As those pyramidal and perpendicular pillars (*r*) had epitaphs expressing the name and rank of the deceased, so Christians imitated such examples by their grave-stones and tombs. # MONASTICON HIBERNICUM.

In a country where the clergy were as nume-
rous as (*s*) all the other claſſes of men, and thoſe
for the moſt part Monks, an account of their or-
ders and their various eſtabliſhments includes no
ſmall ſhare of the general hiſtory of the nation.
About the middle of the fourth century Mona-
chiſm was introduced into Italy, and quickly
ſpread through the Weſt. The (*t*) biographers of
St. Patrick tell us, he learned monaſtic diſcipline
under Martin biſhop of Tours ; a prelate who
had no leſs than two (*u*) thouſand Monks in a mo-
naſtery contiguous to his cathedral. Our apoſtle
ſtudied this faſhionable proſeſſion for many years
among the Italian aſcetics, and his predilection for
it was conſpicuous when he formed the Iriſh
church. In ſucceeding centuries theſe foundations
multiplied amazingly, ſo that at the reformation,
there were five hundred and twenty-nine monaf-
teries and nunneries in this kingdom.

The Monasticon Hibernicum, the writings of
Ware, Allemande and others, are too ſhort to
give ſatisfaction on ſo ample a ſubject. Doctor
King archbiſhop of Dublin, who knew the value
of it, did not think it beneath his attention to
make large (*w*) compilations from original records

## ARCHITECTURE.

The buildings of the antient Iriſh were the ſame
as thoſe of every uncivilized people; conſiſting of
materials the ſlighteſt and the eaſieſt to be procured.
Sir James Ware and his followers have fully ſtated
this evidence, and there dropt the ſubject, leaving
an impreſſion upon the reader, as if there were no
other ſtructures in Ireland but ſtraw-built cottages.
This among other things has countenanced that
idea of barbariſm, ſo conſtantly inculcated in books
of geography and travels; and is, in reality, as
glaring a falſhood as any to be found in ſuch inju-
dicious, flimſy and wretched productions. It is
certainly not amiſs to recur to the earlieſt uſages of
nations, but why ſtop there? Is it not as pleaſing
an inveſtigation, to trace the progreſs of know-
ledge from its ſimpleſt exertions to its moſt refin-
ed energies? The different ſtages of architecture
mark, in deciſive characters, the ſtate of civility:
nor is there one topic, in the antiquities of a king-
dom, productive of more elegant entertainment,
or more uſeful information.
   In the enſuing diſſertation, the ſtyle of our an-
tient habitations, and the dawnings of its improve-
ment are given from apparently indiſputable au-
thority.

The writer also introduces, as collateral to the foregoing, the history of our Stone-Crosses, and an inquiry, whether our antient churches resembled the Greek temples. A paradox is also solved, of a nation warmly cultivating the arts and sciences, and yet neglecting architecture ; which was the case of Ireland in certain ages. This will be followed by the—*history and antiquities of Glendaloch, and its Seven Churches, in the county of Wicklow* ;—wherein many of the facts and observations, in the preceding treaties, will be further elucidated and confirmed.

The knowledge of perspective and a taste for drawing, so generally diffused at present, have rescued many unheeded and mouldering objects from total decay, and enriched every collection with beautiful specimens of our antient buildings.

loran thinks our apostle might ordain ninety-six bishops, and as many of these might have died during his long life, and so many succeeded in their room, as completed the number above.

All this is mere conjecture : the solution of the difficulty arises from considering the state and practices of the early christian church. From Clemens Romanus we learn, that in his time, the episcopal order was very numerous ; every (c) city, village, and region had a bishop ; many cities had two and some more. Thus, (d) Alexander and Narcissus were bishops of Jerusalem together ; Paulinus and Miletus of Antioch ; Theodosius and Agapetus of Synada, and Valerius and Augustine of Hippo. The custom for a city to have but one bishop, was first begun in Alexandria, as Epiphanius remarks. So much had the <term>chorepiscopi</term> or village-bishops increased, that it became necessary to restrain their number, which was done in the Laodicean council, in A. D. 367, and before in the Antiochean.

In the fourth century, St. Basil writes to Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, that he did not approve of his multiplying bishops, as thereby the dignity went into contempt : it would be better, adds he, to choose some man worthy a bishoprick, who might take priests to his assistance, than divide a small

By the fifty-eighth Neo-Cæsarean canon, made in A. D. 315, the administration of the sacraments were in a great measure, confined to the bishops and chorepiscopi; and in (*e*) Tertullian it is expressly declared, that presbyters had not the liberty of baptizing without the bishop's permission; or of preaching in some churches, as Socrates assures us. Leo, in his ninety-second epistle, desires Maximus, bishop of Antioch, to hinder monks and laymen from preaching, which was solely the bishop's office. In England, by the third of archbishop Cuthbert's canons in A. D. 747, the bishop is enjoined to visit his parish once a year, and preach the word of God which it *rarely* hears. These last words refer as well to the paucity of clergymen then, as to the restriction of this duty to the bishop. Similar canons may be found in the legatine council of Cealchythe, in A. D. 785, and in Odo's, in A. D. 943.

**GREEK LANGUAGE.** Virgil, our countryman, was one of eight (i) Irish bishops, who undertook, agreeable to the devotion of the times, a journey to the Holy-land. In France he was appointed to a see, by pope Stephen and king Pepin. The latter detained him in his family for two years, to profit by his uncommon erudition and piety. He was afterwards promoted to the bishoprick of Saltzburg, by Otilo, duke of Bavaria, wherein he remained to the time of his death in the year 785. We are told he concealed his rank for some time, and had with him a bishop, named Dobdan, a Greek, who followed him from Ireland. I should wonder, says Usher, at a Grecian's going from Ireland, did I not know, that at Trim in Meath is a church called the Greek church, at this day, A. D. 1632. The learned primate has thrown no further light on this matter, but it will not appear extraordinary when we consider, that (k) Johannes Scotus Erigena, some years after, gave the clearest demonstration of his proficiency in this language by his translation of Dionysius Areopagita, which he dedicated to Charles the Bald, king of France.

**BROGUES WORN WITH HAY IN THEM.** At this day the practice is universal for the natives to have their brogues stuffed with hay or straw, without being able to assign any reason for the custom : the following is offered both as curious and satisfactory. Linnæus tells (o) us, the Laplanders, through their long and cold winters keep abroad with their herds of Rhen-deer : that they never experience kibes, or other effects of intense frosts, by means of this precaution. In summer they cut and dry the slender-eared, broad-leaved cyperus grass, *carex vesicaria* ; this they comb and rub in their hands, and then place it in their shoes so as to cover their feet and legs ; their shoes are made of the skin of the Rhen-deer, the hairy part turned inward ; they have no stockings, their breeches are of the same skin and come down to their ankles. This grass keeps off the cold in winter, and in summer prevents the effects of perspiration.

In like manner, an (p) eye-witness informs us, that the English, when they first settled in America, used the bastard *calamus aromaticus* to keep their feet warm. The antient brogue was made of raw, or half-tanned leather, of one entire piece, and gathered round the foot by a thong ; such an one was found in the year 1770, at Aghaboe, in a bog

## CREAGHTS.

The manners and cuſtoms of rude nations are nearly the ſame in all parts and all ages of the world. The Scythians, according to (*q*) Herodotus and Juſtin, had neither houſes nor fixed ſettlements; they wandered through the country with their flocks and herds. Their wives, their children and little furniture they carried in carts or waggons, covered with ſkins. They were ſtrangers to agriculture. These manners were realized in our Creaghts, and that ſo late as in the laſt century, as appears by this entry in counſellor Harris’s collections, now in the library of the Dublin Society.

> “ Orders by the general aſſembly of confederate Catholics, at Kilkenny, the 12th of Nov. 1647.
>

## A
# DISSERTATION
### ON THE
# ROUND TOWERS
### IN
# IRELAND.

Among the many curiofities of nature and art, with which this kingdom remarkably abounds, not one of them merits a more particular attention than the numerous, slender round towers every where found; and which from the obscurity of their origin, and the uncertainty of their use, have opened to men of leisure and erudition, a spacious field for hypothesis and conjecture.

It is worth remarking, that men blindly devoted to systems too often deal unfairly by the authors to whom they are most indebted; they select such parts as make for their argument; in these no error or imperfection appears; but those that contravene their favourite notions are reprobated as undeserving the least regard; not considering, that by invalidating the credibility and authority of a writer

<vocab>Ireland, round towers, antiquities, archaeology, hypothesis, systems</vocab>

<page-type>text</page-type>

<header>A DISSERTATION ON THE</header>

writer in any instance, they must defeat the purpose for which they adduce him. Giraldus Cambrensis hath remarkably experienced this treatment ; in some cases his testimony is alledged as decisive, when in others he is said to be fabulous and prejudiced ; yet if we allow for the age in which he lived ; the prevalence of romantic fiction ; the low state of learning and criticism, with a tincture of personal vanity ; we shall see him throughout his works, a man of excellent talents, and well versed in the various departments of science then known and cultivated. His coming to this kingdom at different times, with his continuance in it, must give a degree of credit to his relations not lightly to be regarded, nor rejected without sufficient reason.

“ The Irish nation, says (*a*) this writer, is inhospitable, living on the produce of their cattle, and leading a life but little superior to them ; nor have they emerged from the pastoral state. As the progress of human society is to advance from woods to open fields, and from the latter to towns, this nation despising agriculture, inattentive to civil wealth and regardless of law, spend their lives in woods and pastures.”—These remarks are just, and evince the fine philosophical turn of the author ; they are exactly the same ideas which make a conspicuous figure in one of the sketches of (*b*) lord Kaims. The Irish had quitted the hunter, and advanced

<margin>r</margin>Cambrensis proceeds:—“ The (d) different kinds of metal with which the deeper veins abound, through an idle disposition are neither dug for any use, or turned to any account. For gold, which they covet to have in abundance, is imported among them by Ostmen merchants. They have no manufactures of linen, woollen, or other kinds. Sunk in indolence and sloth, they esteem it their highest bliss not to labour, and their greatest riches to enjoy their liberty.” — This and the former citation accord; there are an union and harmony of parts, which show the pencil of the painter was guided by truth in the great outline. It is scarcely possible to conceive, as it would be very preposterous to assert, that the writer rather indulged a licentious fancy on this occasion, than represented living manners; the most perverse nationality must blush to assert it.

The gold imported by the Ostmen was used by the natives for personal ornaments. They beheld these strangers decorated with this shining metal, worked into (e) bracelets, rings and other garnitures, as badges of nobility, and rewards of valour, and they were eager to adorn themselves in like manner. Coined money was not (f) common in the tenth century among the northern nations, and out of the English pale the Irish had very little.

Even so late as the year 1331, it appears by (g) record, that fines or law-mulcts were ordered to be paid no longer in cattle but in money; and in 1399, the prince of Leinster’s horse was valued at four hundred cows. The gentleman who attended king Richard II. in his expedition hither at this time, adds:—(h) For in that country they barter by exchange, and one commodity for another, and not for ready money.—If then permutation was in use in 1399, the Irish were surely not more improved in 1185, when Cambrensis was here and examined the country! So that we may give full credit to his narration in this respect, notwithstanding what our antiquarians tell us of the vast treasures of our monarchs.

Cambrenſis having ſhown, that the dawnings of commerce among the Iriſh originated from their intercourſe with the Oſtmen, intimates alſo other arts, with which thoſe foreigners brought them acquainted, and particularly that moſt uſeful one of maſonry. The Celtic nations did not know (*i*) the uſe of lime or cements, and the reaſon is obvious ; they were in a rude and diſperſed ſtate, without fixed habitations or domeſtic improvements ; and timber abounded for every purpoſe. In America moſt of the public and private buildings are of wood, as well as the ſmall fortreſſes in remote parts. It was the ſcarcity of timber, and the danger of wooden houſes from fire in populous towns, that made mankind turn their attention to more durable materials, and borrow the arts of more civilized nations.

This neceſſity had not operated in favour of Iriſh architecture at this time, nor for ſome ages after the arrival of the Oſtmen ; who at firſt introduced themſelves here as traders, if we believe Cambrenſis, but more probably as (*k*) pirates, infeſting and trading alternately along the coaſts of the kingdom, as circumſtances offered. This was in the year 795. Succeſs allured others to ſimilar enterprizes. Finding the country open and fertile, and the inhabitants in no ſituation to oppoſe large bodies, they attempted the conqueſt of them. England, Scotland and (*l*) France had felt the force of the

About the middle of the eighth century, pope
Stephen III. built a (z) tower on the church of
St. Peter at Rome, and placed in it three bells;
and yet such towers were not common in France
and the West at a much later period, as appears
from an antient (a) writer, whose expressions leave
no doubt, that they were separate buildings from
the church and their erection very unusual. About
the end of the ninth century (A. D. 874) the (b)
Greek church adopted bells from the Venetians;
their belfry also (c) was distinct from the church.
The Turks who imitated the Christians in many of
their religious practices, did the same in this of the
tower, and by it they formed their (d) minarets.
In the beginning of the eighth century the Saracens
settled in Spain, and in the next age, the northern
rovers, by us called Ostmen and by the conti-
nental people Normans, began to be formidable,
to commit depredations and to establish settlements
on the French and Spanish coasts as well as in

<meta>catchword: That</meta>

Ireland. In these expeditions they must have seen the Christian and Saracenic belfries, and brought back the ideas of them on their return ; why then it may be asked are they not found in England?

England in the seventh century commenced an elegant style of building in her principal churches and monastic foundations, under the patronage of Wilfrid, Biscopius and others. They were followed by several other prelates and abbots in proportion to their power and opulence. In the year 935, their taste was so much improved, that (*e*) cross-ailes and high towers were added to religious edifices. But the round tower, which was a Danish work, could not find place in England, because the domination of these northerns was not established there until half a century after the introduction of cross-ailes ; by which time the Anglo-Saxon style was going into disuse, and almost sunk in the Gothic or Norman. Had the Danes reared their towers before those elegant structures, the meanest peasant would have ridiculed the attempt. But in Ireland the case was totally different ; our churches were of wood, and as mean as possible ; a bell was wanting (which they could not admit) to collect people to divine worship, who were generally settled in the vicinity of the church ; and it also served to give an alarm in times of danger. Cambrensis calls them ecclesiastical towers, which fixes their appropriation, as the Irish do (*f*) Cloghad, or belfries.

That they are Danish works their rotund figure
manifestly evinces; this was the (g) form of their
camps and fortifications, of their barrows and stone
circles, (h) and of their antient habitations still existing.

"It is unquestionably certain, says (i) the learned
Dr. Macpherson, that the oldest forts on the western
and northern coasts of Scotland, were erected by
the barbarians of the northern Europe. All the
Norwegian towers in the *Ebudes* were of a *circular*
form; the old square castles there are of a much
later date."—The opinion of a (k) respectable native
writer deserves notice: "It is most certain, that
those high, round, narrow towers of stone, built
cylinder-wise, whereof Cambrensis speaks, were
never known or built in Ireland, as indeed no
more were any castles, houses, or even churches of
stone, at least in the north of Ireland, before the
year of Christ 838, when the heathen Danes pos-
sessing a great part of that country, built them in
several places, to serve as watch-towers against the
natives. Though ere long the Danes being ex-
pulsed, the Christian Irish turned them to another,
and much better, because an holy use, that is to
steeple-houses or bell-fries; from which latter use
made of them it is, that ever since to this present,
they are called in Irish *cloghteachs*, that is, bell-
fries or bell-houses; *cloc* or *clog* signifying a bell,
and *teach* a house in that language."

In an antient Irish manuscript (says the (l) historian of the county of Cork) containing some annals of Munster, there is mention made of the building the tower of Kineth in this county, about the year 1015, soon after the celebrated battle of Clantarffe. This is too late a period to make it the era of their general erection by at least a century ; but it does not weaken the probability of both Danes and natives continuing the practice of building such structures until nearly the time of the Norman invasion, that is, until an improved taste in architecture took place, which was about that time. Mr. Brereton imagines, (m) these towers to be places from whence the people were called to worship by the sound of some wind instrument. This notion arose from an iron trumpet being found in one of them ; if this circumstance be really true, it is a new proof of their being Danish works, though the inference deduced may be doubtful. The author last cited asserts, that these towers preceded the use of bells in Ireland ; this is conjecture without the least proof ; bells were used in the ceremonies (n) of religion as early as the fifth century, and these towers were constructed about the tenth.

Whether there are any round towers in Denmark or Norway is not positively decided ; we have no evidence of accurate inquiries being made after them ; for cursory questions put to ignorant natives, or the reports of superficial observers will never

Mr. *Pennant* (o) tells us, that while he lay in the sound of *Jona* in the *Hebrides*, two gentlemen from the isle of *Mull*, and who had possessions there, seemed to know nothing of that astonishing curiosity, the Basaltic isle of *Staffa*. Nor is it less remarkable, that until a mercurial (p) traveller enumerated those in this kingdom, they had been before but slightly noticed by our historians, topographers and antiquaries, though more than forty of them, and those well preserved, still remain. The same may be said of the Swedish antiquities, which were but imperfectly known until *Dahlberg* lately exhibited many of them in his *Suecia Hodierna et Antiqua*.

But the late reception of Christianity will very well account for the want of round towers, or other antient monuments of religion, in northern Europe. The *Normans*, *Danes*, *Swedes* and their neighbours did not embrace (q) the doctrine of redemption until the twelfth century. At that time the more southern nations were tolerably civilized; sumptuous edifices dedicated to sacred uses, were common among them, the antient being mouldered into ruins, or sunk into oblivion; even had they survived,

survived, no one would dream of making them models of imitation.

After all, these structures might have been peculiar to Ireland, and Cambrensis intimates as much when he says, they were built *patrio more*, after the fashion of the country. The circular Norwegian towers, mentioned above by Dr. Macpherson, might have suggested the idea of them, and their appropriation to religious purposes arose from the state of Christianity then in this kingdom. When once they were adopted, they soon were multiplied.

Mr. Pennant, speaking of the Scottish round towers, says they could not be intended for belfries, because they are placed near the steeples of churches, infinitely more commodious for that end. This supposes the steeples and round towers to be coeval, which is not the case; our ancestors, whatever may be thought of them at this day, were incapable of committing such a solecism in architecture. Though the tower was used as a belfry, yet this by no means superceded the necessity of steeples on stone-buildings of later construction; such structures, being generally in the form of a cross, had a steeple raised on its intersection. Thus in the cemetery of the cathedral of St. Canice, Kilkenny, there is a beautiful round tower; yet the symmetry of the cathedral, which is Gothic, required a steeple, and it has one. Wherever we find a round tower, we may be certain the church contiguous to it is of early antiquity, and not later than the eleventh century.

A learned (r) antiquary is of opinion, that these towers were erected by the *Phenicians* or *Carthaginians* in their trading voyages hither ; some passages in antient authors seem to countenance this conjecture. *Diodorus Siculus*, (s) discoursing of the *Hyperboreans* who inhabited an island opposite the *Celtic* region, says :

> " The trees there bear fruit twice every year. The fabulous chronicle records, that *Latona* was born in that country ; hence the inhabitants adore *Apollo*, whose praises they are continually chanting. In the isle is a noble forest, dedicated to this deity, a temple also of a *spherical* figure, filled with presents, and a city sacred to the same God ; the greatest part of the people are musicians, they play on the harp in his temple, and sing hymns to his praise."

This description is plainly the work of fancy ; the author is not to be censured, when he himself intimates a suspicion of his authority.

<margin>(t) *Travels into Persia*, part 2. chap. 43.</margin>

The opinion acquiesced in for some years, is that of the late reverend dean Richardson, and since adopted and improved by Mr. Harris, in his edition of Sir James Ware's antiquities. This supposes our towers to be the residence of anachorite monks, and imitations of the eastern pillars; and is founded on the account Evagrius gives of Simeon Stylites, which, to avoid ambiguity, it may be proper to (z) extract:

> "The fabrick of Simeon’s church represents the form of a cross, beautified with porticoes of four sides; opposite these are placed pillars, curiously made of polished stone, whereon the roof is gracefully raised to an height. In the midst of these porticoes is an open court, wrought with much art, in which court stands the *pillar*, forty cubits high, whereon that incarnate angel upon earth (Simeon) led a celestial life."

It must require a warm imagination to point out the similarity between this pillar and our tower. The one was solid, the other hollow; the one was square, and the other circular.

We are told by Mr. Smith (*d*) that he once believed thoſe towers to be the retreats of anachorites; but from new information, derived from an Iriſh manuſcript, he now thinks they were places of penance. The penitent mounted on the higheſt loft, performed there a probation of ſome days; in like manner he proceeded to the next ſtage, and ſo downwards until he finiſhed his religious courſe, when he was received at the door of the tower, (which faced the weſtern door of the church) by the clergy and people. And he credits this notion, as it coincides with the general poſition of the doors of theſe towers, which are always to the eaſt ; but the poſition is poſitively otherwiſe, as will preſently be ſeen in thoſe of Abernethy and Brechin, nor is any general rule obſerved in placing the doors, as he muſt have known from examining many of them in the counties he deſcribes. It was therefore very diſingenuous to ſacrifice his veracity in ſupport of a groundleſs hypotheſis, and an anonymous manuſcript, eſpecially as he himſelf ſupplies the ſtrongeſt proof of their original deſignation in (*e*) another work, where he remarks, that the round tower of Ardmore had been uſed for a belfry, there being towards the top, not only four windows to let out the ſound, but alſo three pieces of oak, ſtill remaining, on which the bell was hung. And Mr. Pennant informs us, the tower of Brechin is uſed for a belfry ; as is that of Roſcrea. This evidence ſeems deciſive ; it is truth confirmed by immemorial uſage, and triumphing over learned whims.

## SHEAN CASTLE.

IN the earlier ages of ſociety, the wants of mankind and their provocations to injuries ſeem to have been few ; and yet ambition and jealouſy too frequently called forth the ferocity of untamed nature and the exertions of brutal force ; diſturbed the ſavage inhabitants of the wilderneſs, and compelled them to ſeek ſecurity on (a) eminences, and in places of difficult acceſs ; to incloſe an area with a ditch ; or form an abatis of trees. Convenience and emergency pointed out theſe different modes of defence, and this kingdom is full of thoſe antient fortreſſes. Separated from the chain of neighbouring hills, and precipitous on all ſides, except to the ſouth-weſt, Dunamaſe offered a ſafe aſylum to the firſt poſſeſſor ; and if any

reliance is to be placed on its *(b)* name, it was a place of strength in the remotest times.

Dûn na maes in Celtic is—The Fort of the Plain.—The plain, is the Great-Heath of Maryborough, lying to the north-east of the Dûn; a flat of considerable extent. Ptolemy makes Dunum an inland Irish town, but *(c)* Cambden places it in Ulster, and says it is Downpatrick. Ware *(d)* believes the British antiquary hath assigned it an improper situation, which supposition of Ware’s, Harris doth not contradict. But the latter writers are certainly mistaken; for Dunamase, from the narrowness of its circumference, never could contain but a few cabbins, and in records it is constantly mentioned as a fortress; whereas Downpatrick, as Cambden rightly observes, was a very old town, an episcopal see, and memorable on other accounts; besides, Ptolemy’s information was very imperfect as to the interior of the island, but tolerably accurate as to what respects the sea-coast.

Mr. Pennant, in his tour in Scotland, saw, near Struan, a Danish fortification on the top of a rock; about a furlong distant, was another large fortified rock; these fortresses, he adds, are universally called, in the Erse, Dûns. There are two Dûns in the Queen’s County, and the same in every circumstance as the Scottish ones; this of Dunamase, the other at Clopoke, about five miles distant. They are conoid hills of limestone, exhibiting a very singular appearance, and not only tenable by a small garrison, but before the use of artillery, almost impregnable.

mase, as we shall presently see. Finglas, by mentioning Dunamase alone, intimates that it was the chief residence or mansion of the family in those parts ; and agreeable to this idea and its importance, Sir John Davis calls it—the principal house of Lord Mortimer in Leix.

As it bounded the English pale on the west, a strong castle was built there to protect the vicinity ; it was the residence of the (1) seneschal, who represented the lord ; and the seat of military authority and civil jurisdiction ; here all the incidents of the feudal system were discharged, and hither the tenants resorted for justice and protection. The precise time of erecting this castle cannot be ascertained, but it may be conjectured to have been about the beginning of Henry III's reign, in the year 1216 ; for nearly at the same time, the castle of Ley, eight miles distant, was erected by the barons of Ophaly, on the banks of the Barrow ; a structure, in the thickness and height of its walls, its vaults and disposition of rooms, and its general style of building, resembling the former.

As the lord Paramount was bound by the feudal constitution to provide the state, on every occasion, with a certain number of soldiers ; to answer such emergencies, and to secure his property against the

In the year 1329, under the government of Sir John Darcy, Dunamase and other castles were recovered from the Irish; but such at that time was the debility of the English administration in this kingdom, that there was very little security for property against the rapacity of the first invader. The O Mores again seized on Dunamase, about the 18th of Edward the Third, but were dispossessed in two years after; for by a (n) plea-roll of the 20th of Edward the Third it appears, that Connel O More of Leix, who after rebellion had submitted himself at Athy to Walter Bermingham, justiciary of Ireland, acknowledged that he held his manor of Bellet and other his lands in Leix, of Roger Mortimer, as of his manor of Donmaske (Dunamase).

On the retreat of Ormond, these forts (p) submitted to general Preston, but were re-taken by the king’s forces, and continued in their possession until the year 1646, when Owen Roe O Neil entered the Queen’s county, committing every act of outrage and cruelty; he (q) took Dysart, Maryborough, Cullenbrack, Sheehen alias Dsiden, Belaroyn, Castlereban, &c. Dunamase within a small mile of Dysart did not escape.

In 1648, O Neil offered to surrender his garrisons in the Queen’s county to colonel Jones, and to lay down his arms, provided he and the confederate catholics might have the privileges confirmed to them which they enjoyed in the reign of king James; but this was not accepted; the next year lord Castlehaven drove O Neil out of the county.

In July 1650, Maryborough, Dunamase, and the neighbouring forts surrendered to the colonels Heuson and Reynolds; Dunamase was blown up and effectually dismantled, as were the rest.

On each side of the barbican were ditches, as far as the hill was accessible, and the (*r*) outward ballium was flanked with two towers or bastions; the first gateway is seven feet wide, and the walls six feet thick; it has a (*s*) machicolation over it, for pouring down melted lead or scalding water; the wall of this ballium is a parapet, crenellated, and to the N. E. is twenty feet high, with long chinks and oillet holes. The distance between tower and tower is one hundred and seventy-four feet.

Between the outward and inward ballia is a length of one hundred feet; the gate of the latter is placed in a tower, and over it was a guard-room; in the thickness of the walls are side passages admitting but one person at a time, and he by no means corpulent. From this second tower begins the parapet wall that surrounds the summit of the hill; its circumference is 1086 feet; the area is not perfectly circular, though nearly so, as far as the projections and inequalities of the rock will admit; so that its diameter at top is 362 feet. The hill is naturally an elliptical conoid; in some parts, from its base to its vertex, it measures 200 feet.

Contiguous to this was a dwelling house, seventy-two feet long and twenty-one wide ; on this were platforms and embattled parapets, from whence the garrison might see and command the exterior works. The house was divided into apartments, and vaults ran under the whole. To the N. W. was a well of excellent water ; and on the west was, what tradition calls, a prison ; but it seems to have been a postern. The naked rock appears on the N. E. side, and the approach to the other parts was difficult and dangerous. When whole and complete it was a beautiful model of military architecture, and even at this day presents the curious visitant with noble ruins of its former grandeur.

Small silver coins, belonging to the early Irish princes, have been found at Dunamase ; there is one in the collection of the Rev. Mervyn Archdall, rector of Attier-Attanagh, in the diocese of Ossory, that is a great curiosity ; it is the size of a silver four-pence, but thinner ; on the face is this epigraphe—Re Morrah, King O Mora ; or O More ; and on the reverse is, Na Dunegh, or rather Dunadh, of the Fort ; expressing the place of coinage, and the residence of the chief. The letters are the antient <term>Ogham croabh</term> characters, and the same with those that appear on the coins of O Toole, found at Glendaloch in the county of Wicklow. This coin was struck in the eleventh century ; for,

### S H E A N  C A S T L E,

As we before observed, was a manor dependent on Dunamase, and built not many years posterior to it. The name is variously written. In a record of the 20 Richard II. A. D. 1397, it is Sion; and in a $(t)$ tract relative to the Irish rebellion, it is Sheehan; but as the most antient name generally approaches nearest the true one, so *sion* in Irish expresses its exposure to all the vicissitudes of weather, it standing on an high eminence and unsheltered.

In an account of the castles in the Queen's county in 1615, it is called Shian; and on the banks of the Blackwater near Lismore, in the county of Waterford, is a Shian castle; but the $(u)$ writer who gives this information offers nothing in explanation of the appellation.

It has escaped the notice of our antiquaries, that the English on their settlement here, gave Saxonic names to places, which have passed with the incurious for Irish ones, and therefore their etymology is in vain sought for in the latter language; thus the name of the third cantred of the barony of Ossory, in the Queen's county, is Upperwoods; intimating its forests mounted on its lofty mountains. The parish,
