parish, which comprehends the whole cantred, is called Offerelane, corrupted from Oferlyng, which in Saxon means superior, and is synonymous to Upper-woods. Shean might originally have been Sien, the Saxon Seon, the pupil or sight of the eye, it bearing this analogy to Dunamase. The English spoke almost pure Saxon in the reign of Henry II. which gives countenance to the preceding conjecture.

Shean castle is situated on one of those high conical hills, which are so common in its vicinity. Though not remarkable for its magnitude, it was a place of considerable strength; the declivities round it being steep and easily defended. By the (w) record before cited, it appears, that Sir Robert Preston in the year 1397, held by the law of England, the inheritance of Margaret his late wife the manor of Sion in Liex, of Roger Mortimer, as of his manor of Dunmaske (Dunamase); it shared the revolutions of the latter in the subsequent periods of history; but being neither so strong or tenable it escaped demolition, and continued for centuries in its pristine state, until it came into possession of its present occupier, the reverend doctor Charles Coote, dean of Kilfenora.

He has revived Shean with new splendor, and added at a vast expence, such embellishments to its fine situation, as make it both an ornament to the country and a delightful residence.

## WRITING
### USED BY THE
## IRISH
### IN THEIR PAGAN STATE, AND AFTER THEIR CONVERSION TO CHRISTIANITY.

IT has been much controverted in the Republic of Letters, whether the ancient inhabitants of Ireland, before their converſion to the Chriſtian faith, had the uſe of Letters, or any means of communicating their thoughts in writing. If we give credit to their antiquaries and hiſtorians, no people cultivated learning with ſo much aſſiduity, and that at a period when the Greeks and Romans remained in a’ ſtate of barbariſm. According to them (a), the art of writing was known in this iſland as early as the tenth century before the Chriſtian

Notwithstanding the circumſtantial account given by the antiquaries and hiſtorians of the middle and latter ages, relative to the learning and civilization of the antient Iriſh, the learned in general have been much divided on this head; as the teſtimonies hitherto given, have rather been poſitive aſſertions, unſupported by proofs and matters of fact, than real hiſtories. For though they have made frequent mention of ſeveral ſpecies of letters and alphabets, made uſe of by the pagan inhabitants of this iſland, yet they have given very few ſpecimens of the characters, and none before their converſion to the Chriſtian faith. And though they alſo make frequent mention of ancient writings or records, from which their more modern hiſtories are ſuppoſed to be taken, few if any of theſe records have come down to our time. These authorities appear sufficient to overthrow intirely the pretension of the Irish historians, relative to the learned state of their pagan ancestors ; as the Britons who, according to Strabo, resorted to Rome (*h*) could not be ignorant of the internal state of this island ; and from whom we may reasonably conclude both Strabo and Mela obtained their information concerning the Irish. And in the days of Tacitus, the ports of Ireland were well known (*i*); consequently, that celebrated historian could not be ignorant of the real character of its inhabitants. But Solinus had a better opportunity than either Strabo, Mela, or Tacitus, of obtaining information on this subject ; as in his time, Britain had been a province of the empire at least 200 years. Some communication must have been maintained between the two islands during that period, and consequently the Romans could not have remained ignorant of the manners and customs of the inhabitants of Ireland.

Seeing therefore the most respectable authorities, ancient and modern, agree in excluding not only the Irish, but all the Celtic tribes in general from an early knowledge of letters, it may be thought presumptuous to attempt the establishment of a contrary opinion. But we ought not to be deterred by the authority of great names, however respectable, from searching after truth; for though those whom we have quoted and many others, have declaimed against the use of letters among the aboriginal inhabitants of Europe, yet there are several who have maintained the contrary. Laertius in his life of Aristotle, and in his discourse on philosophy, says, that the Greeks had the original of their theology, and the most sublime parts of their philosophy from the druids of the Celtes (*n*). And J. Magnus asserts (*o*), that the northern inhabitants of Europe had the art of expressing things by writing, long before the Latins invented letters; and that the aboriginals of Italy, whom the Romans expelled on their settlement therein, though rude, had the knowledge of letters and taught them to their conquerors. Even the Goths in a very early period, engraved characters or letters on large stones,

hieroglyphics, in their hiero-grammatic writings,
or those which treated of their religion, philosophy
and laws.

The method of describing the human thoughts
by the representation of the several objects of
nature, seems to have been the first effort of the
mind towards transmitting the knowledge of past
transactions to posterity. At what period therefore
this invention took its rise is impossible to determine;
it probably was during the infant state of society,
as the practice of writing by means of pictures and
symbols was universal, not only among all the
nations of antiquity, but even such among the

The druids distinguished the active principle or
fire by the name of *tis*, *dis*, or *teut* and teutates;
that is, the *He* or masculine principle, who by its
action on the earth, whom they considered the
Mother of Nature, causes it to produce the several
species of animals and vegetables. The earth there-
fore was the passive principle, which in this case
they frequently called *ops* or *opis*, from the Celtic
*op* to cry out, from whence *opeigh* a crier, alluding
to the cries of a mother in labour ; the earth being
supposed to labour, in bringing forth her various
productions, as a woman in child-birth (*b*); whence
we may reasonably conclude, that the Egyptian
*Osiris*, the Celtic *Dis*, *Tis* or *Teut* were the same,
and signified the universal spirit or active principle,
which the ancients understood to be fire ; also the
Egyptian *Isis*, the Greek *Ceres*, and the Celtic *Ops*
were of the same import, and represented the earth
or nature in general. The character therefore we
are now speaking of, as it bears so great a resem-
blance to those in the Bembine tables representing
the earth or nature, undoubtedly among the druids
was of the same signification. It seems also to
have been retained by the ancient Irish, long after
their conversion to Christianity, in the form of
No. 6, to represent Jesus Christ the Saviour of the
World ; in which sense it stands on all the Irish coins.

## No. 7,

Is a sort of Trellis-work found on one of the tabernacles at the mount of New-Grange, and on several stones and crosses both in Ireland and Britain. Trellis-work or small lozenges; amongst the ancient Britains, Germans and indeed all the aboriginals of Europe, signified fate, providence, chance, or fortune. It seems to have been derived from a species of divination used by the Scythic and Celtic tribes, consisting of long quadrangular pieces of wood taken from fruit trees ; these pieces had several symbolic characters engraven on them, when, being in the act of divining, they were thrown across ; as the several characters fell and answered to each other, the auspices were taken (*c*). These pieces of wood called by the Scythæ *run-stobs* and by the Irish *ogham croabh*, that is, the staves and furrows of wisdom, were retained many centuries after the establishment of Christianity, and their position in divining frequently drawn on crosses and the walls of churches, as emblems of the Divine Providence ; nay, the divination itself was retained in some parts of England to the present century (*d*).

By the few characters hitherto diſcovered it is extremely probable, that the weſtern Celtic tribes as well as the Iriſh received their ſymbols from the Carthaginian and Phœnician traders; though poſſibly they might have had ſome ſort of hieroglyphic writing in an earlier period; however, it is more than probable, that the uſe of letters was not known among them long before the Punic merchants viſited their coaſts.

The invention of letters or alphabetic characters have by ſome been placed prior to that of hieroglyphics and ſymbols; but if we conſider, that they were the laſt effort of the human mind, in order to accompliſh an effectual method of tranſmitting the ideas to future ages, we ſhall be inclined to place their diſcovery in much later periods. If they had been the invention of the antediluvians, or of equal ſtanding with hieroglyphics, as ſome learned perſons have imagined, all the nations of the earth would moſt probably have been converſant with them, whereas the contrary is ſufficiently evinced. All the ſocieties of mankind, in the different periods of time, at a certain ſtage of civilization, had the method of expreſſing their thoughts by hieroglyphics if not ſymbols; but letters were confined among the ancients as among the moderns, to not only a particular, but in a great meaſure the very ſame part of the globe. The only nations of antiquity who underſtood this divine art, were the Egyptians, the Libyans, the Ethiopians, the Arabians, the Indoſtans, the Medes, the Perſians, the Syrians, the Hebrews, the Phœnicians, the Celtæ, the weſtern Scythæ, the Greeks and Romans;

comprehending the present Europe, the north and north-east parts of Africa, and the south and western parts of Asia; the only part, of the world at this day which have the knowledge of alphabet characters, except the European colonies in America and Africa, within the last century.

Egypt therefore, as she was the parent of the several arts and sciences which illuminated the ancient world, probably gave birth to letters; a circumstance not only confirmed by the assertion of several of the Greek and Latin writers (i), but further evinced from the remarkable similarity between all the alphabets of antiquity; for the letters contained in the ancient Ethiopic, Arabic, Malabarian, Chaldaic, Samaritan, Phœnician, Punic, Etruscan, Cuphic, Greek and Runic alphabets show evident signs of being derived from one common origin; and several of them, in each alphabet, are actually found as symbols and hieroglyphics, not only in the Ramessean and Bembine tables, but in several inscriptions discovered in the pyramids. To the Egyptians therefore are we indebted for the invention of letters, which they took from their hieroglyphic and symbolic characters; but the time they made this important discovery cannot be determined; it was probably in a very early period; for Moses, who was skilled in all the learning and wisdom of the Egyptians, wrote in alphabetic characters, which he undoubtedly obtained from thence, though they have been long since lost; the present Hebrew letters not being

the same in which the Pentateuch was originally written. But in whatever period Egypt made a discovery so beneficial to the human race in general, it seems to have been the source from which letters proceeded in three distinct channels through the ancient world. The first, taking a northern course, watered the western parts of Asia, and the eastern, southern and midland parts of Europe. The second proceeding westward, enlightened the northern parts of Africa, and in process of time, in conjunction with the first, the western coasts of Europe; whilst the third, being thrown in a south and east direction, furnished the Ethiopians, Arabians and Indians, with the inestimable art. The Egyptian letters, especially during the middle ages of their empire, consisted of three species, that is the literal, the epistolary and hiero-grammatic. In the first were written their scientific works, as philosophy and laws; in the second, their common occurrences of life, and in the third, their religious subjects (k). The several people who visited that country, having been instructed in these methods of writing by the priests, introduced them into their own; where they not only were retained for the aforesaid purposes, but from them and the symbolic characters new alphabets were formed, in which the several species of the Egyptian letters were found, causing thereby the letters of the several nations, though derived from a common origin, to be materially different from each other.

Moses may be considered the father of the northern branch, and the first who brought letters

into the western parts of Asia, though they seem to have made no considerable progress for some time, being confined to the Jewish nation. It was not until about the fourteenth century before the Christian era, when the Canaanites, who fled from Joshua and retired into Egypt, had been expelled that country by Amosis, and settled in Phoenice, that we may date the general introduction of letters into the western parts of Asia ($l$); from Phoenice they proceeded to the Syrians, Ionians and Medes, and were probably those characters mentioned by Pliny, under the name of eternal letters, being the foundation of the Phoenician, Samaritan, Ionian and Chaldaic alphabets. In the beginning of the eleventh century before Christ, the Phoenicians and Syrians, flying under the conduct of Cadmus and other captains from David, introduced letters into Greece and the adjacent countries ($m$); about three hundred years after Cadmus had thus introduced letters, music and poetry among the Greeks, the Medes revolting from the Assyrians, numbers were obliged to seek an asylum in the southern and midland parts of Europe, where they were known for several ages by the name of Sarmatæ or Sar-Madæ, that is descendants of the Medes ($n$); these people, who had obtained the use of letters about four hundred years before their settlement in Europe, probably introduced them among the Celtic and Scythic tribes of the middle regions; where after

Britain therefore may be considered as the grand factory of these traders in this part of the world, and where they had the greatest opportunity of introducing letters, arms, commerce and religion among the natives ; which improvements might be in succeeding ages brought into this country by the British colonies, who fled from the terror of the Roman arms ; if they were not introduced by the Gallic and Iberian merchants, who, on the conquest of Spain and Gaul by the Romans, carried on an extensive trade to Ireland some few years before the Christian era, as we are assured by Tacitus ; who asserts, that in his time the ports of Ireland were better known to foreign merchants than those of Britain (s). In some of the most ancient Irish poems, the arrival of these strangers on the Hibernian coasts is frequently mentioned, to whom subsequent writers have attributed the introduction of letters and several other arts of civil life ; in consequence of which, they assert, that the first grammar of the Irish tongue was written some few years before the birth of Christ by Forchern, who in the compilation, used the Bobeloth character, which they esteem the most ancient form of letters used in

The names and order of these letters have been preserved by the latter writers, especially by Ceanfaolidh, an author of the seventh century, who is said to have transcribed and illustrated Forchern’s grammar ; but whether Ceanfaolidh in his transcript made use of Forchern’s characters, or those of the Latins then in general use throughout the island, we are not informed ; but which ever might have been used for this purpose, the form of the Bobeloth characters have undoubtedly been lost for several centuries, as none of the writers of the latter ages give the least specimen of them.

As little satisfaction therefore as the bare names and order of letters must be, without the characters themselves, yet they have been the means of supplying the defect and negligence of former antiquaries ; and have enabled us, from a number of antient inscriptions found in different parts of the kingdom, and from some MSS. to give the Bobeloth characters complete, as far at least as concerns the alphabet, in the annexed table.

By this table it appears, that the ancient Bobeloth characters of the Irish were all symbols, and bear a great affinity to the Phœnician and Punic, as will be fully shewn in the examination of each particular letter.

The name of the first is *boïbel* or *bobel*, which in the old Celtic, Irish and Punic tongues signifies the chief spirit or ghost, from *bo*, *boi* or *boe* a ghost or apparition, and *bel* a chief or lord ; from whence *Bal* or *Baal* in the Canaanitish, and *Beal* in the

It is evidently derived from the Phœnician and Etruscan Es, and is found in several MSS. of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

The twentieth has the power of I, and is called iachim, which signifies a ladder or steps; the Egyptians used this character to represent a scaling ladder, and the symbol for a siege and architecture in general; as is seen in the Ramessean tables. The character is the old Phoenician and Etruscan I, which was preserved in the British Latin alphabet until the last century. It is probable this character belonged to the ancient pagan British alphabet, if not to that of the Saxon.

These are all the letters given by Antiquaries, as belonging to the Bobeloth alphabet, and are evidently derived from the Phoenician or Punic, and were probably the commercial letters of those people. The order of the Bobeloth alphabet differs indeed materially from all those of antiquity, except the ancient Libyan, between which and the Bobeloth there is a remarkable conformity; especially in the vowels, which in both, are placed at the end, contrary to the orientals, Greeks, Latins and Etruscans. This alphabet was probably the same as the ancient British, mentioned but not specified by the learned Mr. Whitaker, in his history of Manchester; and appears to be the vulgar one used by the Hibernian druids in their common occurrences of life; who from them, after the manner of the ancient Egyptians, Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Libyans and indeed by all the learned nations of antiquity, invented several species of sacred characters to be used with their symbols in their hiero-grammatic writings; in order to prevent their being read either by those of the lower

classes, or by such of the people who understood
the use of letters.

These sacred characters have been much spoken
of by antiquaries, under the denomination of Ogham.
O Flaherty and Harris, in the second volume of his
edition of Ware, have given several specimens of
them; and Sir James Ware relates, that he had a
book written in them on parchment. These charac-
ters they assert were of three species, that is, the
Ogham Croabh, the Ogham Beith, and the Ogham
Coll or Colt, and were used by the druids in the
time of paganism; also by the kings on their coins,
&c. after the establishment of the Christian religion
in the country. They have however been looked
upon by the learned in general in no other light than
cyphers, invented by the monks of the latter ages;
and probably would not have merited any further
consideration, if they were not actually found on
several ancient coins, dug up in several parts of the
kingdom, and in some of the inscriptions at New-
Grange. By these it appears, that the ancient
Ogham consisted only of two species, that is, the
Ogham and Ogham Croabh.

The Ogham was the sacred alphabetic characters
of the druids, so called from the Punic word Ochum
or Hogham, which signifies wisdom; by reason
that all the wisdom of the druids was written in
these characters. The names of the letters of the
Ogham alphabet have been lost for several ages,
but the characters themselves are preserved in some
of the inscriptions in the tumulus at New-Grange,
in the old cathedral of Down, on one of the crosses
at Castle-dermot, and on several British coins.

<vocab>Ogham, Druids, O Flaherty, Harris, Sir James Ware, Ogham Croabh, Ogham Beith, Ogham Coll, New-Grange, Punic, Ochum, Hogham, Castle-dermot, British coins</vocab>

--- Page 210 ---
<language>English</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>196</page-num>
<header>DRUIDISM REVIVED.</header>

They seem to be the characters from whence, in the middle ages, the Christian clergy invented a new alphabet, which they used in ecclesiastical affairs, known in after ages by the name of church text. The Ogham characters, as drawn rudely on stones we have given in table 3.

The Ogham Croabh characters were all upright lines, and appear to be derived from upright stones, the constant simulacres of God and fire amongst all nations of antiquity. They were called Ogham Croabh, or the furrows of wisdom, from the Punic *ogham* wisdom, and the Celtic *croabh* a furrow, and not as has been interpreted by the monks of the latter ages, the *secret branch*.

As the Ogham and Ogham Croabh are words of foreign extraction, probably the characters under these denominations were not the invention of the Hibernian druids, but the sacred characters of the Punic, Phœnician and Egyptian priests, if not of all the heathen priests of antiquity; for Herodotus assures us, that the Greeks and Ionians wrote in characters composed entirely of right lines; and they are actually found in several Egyptian inscriptions. The Goths also wrote in straight lines called by them *run-rhets* or furrows of wisdom.

From the druidic Ogham Croabh, the Irish of the middle and latter ages invented several others. The first is found on the ancient Irish coins, and seems to be derived from the sticks of divination, mentioned in the explanation of the seventh symbol, which were sometimes called the divine-branches; from whence the writers of the latter ages have imagined *ogham croabh* signified the secret-branch.

The power of this Ogham appears to be taken from the Latin alphabet, but in the order of the Bobeloth; which in ſome meaſure evinces, that it was formed after the introduction of Chriſtianity into the iſle.

The ſecond is that given by Harris in his ſecond volume of Ware, and ſhows the foundation of the others, eſpecially the laſt; and was undoubtedly formed from the Hibernian Latin characters, in the order of the Bobeloth; the diphthongs of this Ogham ſeem to have belonged originally to the Bobeloth alphabet.

Theſe are the principal, if not all the alphabetic characters, known to the ancient pagan inhabitants of this iſle, ſome contractions excepted; for we ſhall not ſpeak here of the Ogham Beith and Ogham Coll, they being only cyphers, invented in the latter ages; thoſe who are deſirous of conſulting them, may ſee them explained in the ſecond volume of Harris’s Ware. It will not however be improper to take notice of another alphabet, mentioned by ſeveral antiquaries under the name of the Beithluiſnon, and which they aſſert was the ſecond pagan alphabet, and contained only ſeventeen letters; the names of theſe letters they have given, but not any of the characters, inſtead of which, as in the Bobeloth, they have annexed the Latin characters of the middle ages. On diligent enquiry, we have been able only to diſcover the Beithluiſnon characters on two ſtone croſſes at Caſtle-dermot in the county of Kildare, though an ancient croſs at Sletty in the Queen’s county appears to have been inſcribed with them, but now too much defaced

During the fourth, fifth and sixth centuries, the priests, who were sent to propagate the Christian faith amongst the northern inhabitants of Europe, carried with them not only the Latin tongue but also the letters used during those periods, in Italy and other southern countries; which characters were evidently derived from the ancient Etruscan mixed with the Punic and Libyan; and which, in process of time, laid the foundations of most of the alphabets used in the several countries of Europe during the middle ages, as the Irish, Saxon, German and Gallic.

The letters therefore used by the Irish, both in their manuscripts and printed books, down to the last century, were the Latin characters, introduced by St. Patrick or some other of the Christian missionaries, and were the same as those used through the greatest part of Europe during the middle ages; for which reason Nennius asserts, that the Irish were taught their Abietoria by St. Patrick *(a)*; an assertion from which Bolandus, Ware and Innes, supported by the authority of Tirechan, a writer of the seventh century, have imagined, that the ancient Irish had not the use of letters prior to their acquaintance with the light of the gospel *(b)*. Though the Christian Hibernian characters are evidently derived from the Latin, yet they have been cruelly distorted and mangled in their order and names by the monks of the latter ages, who having lost the form of their Bobeloth and Bethluisnon, applied their names to the Abicetoria, which they put in the order of those ancient characters; but even not content with thus disfiguring them, in order to give them the greater appearance of antiquity, hearing from some of their poems and chronicles that the ancient Irish wrote upon wood and the bark of trees, imagined their letters bore the names of trees; in consequence of which they have interpreted the names of the Bethluisnon to signify so many trees, though they have no such signification in any language upon earth; from whence also, Bobeloth has been interpreted the Wooden Row; an instance of the ignorance and imposition of the monks and antiquaries of the latter ages.

Seeing the Irish and Britons not only before their conversion to the Christian faith, but even before their commerce with the Romans, had the method of expressing their thoughts by means of letters and characters, in common with the other aboriginal inhabitants of Europe; how are we to reconcile such improvements with the assertions of the Roman historians, who have constantly maintained, that none of the barbarians of Europe had the use of

This seeming difficulty however, will in a great measure be overcome, if we consider that not only letters but all knowledge whatever, among the ancient inhabitants of Europe, was intirely confined to a set of people distinguished by the name of druids; these, so far from communicating their knowledge and learning to the people in general, took all possible care to conceal them; alledging, that neither conscience nor religion permitted the laity to read, and that the memory would be greatly impaired if they began to commit their thoughts to writing, for no person would be at the trouble of learning by heart what they could find in every book (*c*); besides their instructions being only for those initiated into the mysteries of the laws and religion of the country, they ought to be held intirely secret, and that it would be really a sacrilege to commit them to public writing, because after that it would be impossible to prevent their doctrine from falling into the hands of strangers. So great an effect had this artful insinuation on the minds of the people, that for several years after their commerce with the Greeks and Romans, nay after their conversion to the Christian faith, they were so far from receiving the knowledge of letters with that avidity their utility deserved, that they constantly neglected and even refused to become acquainted

From these circumstances we cannot be surprized, that the Greek and Roman writers should assert that none of the Celtes had the use of letters ; for though the druids committed the principal tenets of their religion, philosophy and laws to writing, yet as they took all possible care to conceal the books in which these subjects were written, not only from strangers but even from their own people, the ancients had no means of becoming acquainted with the druidic writings.

On what materials therefore the druids wrote, or what were the form of their books, we have not the least authentic information ; but as paper was not invented till the eleventh century $(g)$, nor parchment known in the north of Europe until the Romans had introduced it, it could not have been on these substances. Tacitus says, that the ancient Germans wrote on monuments of stone $(h)$ ; and sculptured stones are mentioned in the poems of Ossian. The Irish antiquaries assert, that their druids wrote on tables of wood and the bark of trees with an iron stile $(i)$ ; a circumstance far from being improbable.

The method of writing on wooden tables is undoubtedly very ancient, it was practised by the Egyptians and Phoenicians ; and we are assured by Plutarch, that the laws which Solon gave to the Athenians, in the course of the forty-sixth olympiad,

Even the present Brahmins of India continue to write their prayers and several other subjects relative to their religion, on thin plates of wood; and the greater part of the aboriginal inhabitants of North America to this day, draw their plans and hieroglyphic writings on the bark of birch; from whence we can scarce have a doubt, that the Celtic druids in general as well as the Irish wrote on these materials.

The form of the Scythic wooden books was that of a square prism, about a foot in length, having the characters engraven on the four sides; but those of the ancient Greeks, Phœnicians and Irish were thin oblong pieces, on which the characters were written with an iron stile after the manner of the Carthaginians, Egyptians and Phœnicians, that is from the left to the right, and from the right to the left alternately, as is evinced from the inscriptions at New-Grange and from several MSS. This method of writing was called by the Greeks *boustrophedon* or the plowed ridges, as it resembled the course of the furrows of the plough; the Irish called it *cionn fa eite*, or the head of the ridge, and *cor fa chasan*, or the reapers path (*l*). The Hibernian Christian clergy frequently wrote in the *cionn fa eite* down to the fourteenth century, though somewhat altered from the ancient; they only using it in the close of a sentence, whilst the ancients used it almost in every other line, writing from the left to the right,

Besides this alternate method of writing, the druids appear to have frequently written their symbols like the Egyptians and Chinese, in perpendicular lines from the top to the bottom ; and it is probable, that the Ogham Croabh was frequently written in this manner.

Though the ancient inhabitants of Ireland undoubtedly received the knowledge of letters either from the Punic or Iberian traders, some few years before the Christian era, yet knowledge was not universal throughout the island for some centuries after. It was not until the middle of the second century that the Hibernian druids committed their poems, laws and philosophy to writing ; when Conor mor or Connachar M<gloss>c</gloss>Nessan, called by the Irish historians Fedlimid and Ollaimfodlah, that is, the wise and learned man, was by the Caël or Tuiath de Danans elected king of the northern parts of Ireland in A. D. 164. This great prince, who was of the druidic order, observing the imperfection of the laws and histories by being retained in the memory only, revived the celebrated convention of Taragh, so much spoken of by the Irish antiquaries, and which had been originally instituted about the middle of the first century for the assembly of the states. In this convention, all poetic compositions relative to history and laws, composed by any of the druidic order, were recited before the general assembly of the chiefs, druids and bards ; such as received their approbation were committed to writing and carefully taught the youths in the several academies throughout the island, over which the druids presided. By the general establishment of the art of writing, by authority, among all orders of the Hibernian druids, we may reasonably conclude, that the druidic books were considerably encreased from the second century, and were numerous on the introduction of Christianity; yet none of their works have come to us, nor even to the eighth century; so indefatigable were the first Christian missionaries in destroying every monument of heathen superstition. Though we ought not to attribute the entire destruction of the druidic literature to the zeal of those who propagated the sacred truths of the gospel among our heathen ancestors; much is owing to the druids themselves, who on embracing the new religion constantly destroyed such of their hiero-grammatic writings as treated of their old; so that from the earnest desire of one party to keep their doctrine an eternal secret, and the zeal of the

The loss of the druidic books may probably be regretted by the curious, and in several instances perhaps, would have been of real utility, yet they might not give us the information we expect. The hiero-grammatic writings, or those which contained the principles of their religion and philosophy, were chiefly written in symbols; a method though useful to those who were masters of the subject, in order to refresh the memory, yet would be almost inexplicable to those not initiated into the mysteries. Their laws and historic poems, being wrote in literary characters, would be the only part of their erudition of use to the moderns; these not being on religious subjects, escaped the fury of the zealots, and remained either in the minds of the people or preserved in the Latin characters, several ages after the druidic order was no more, and many have found their way down almost to our own time. It was from the historic poems of the druids and ancient bards, that O Flaherty and Keating composed their ancient history of Ireland, not indeed immediately from the poems themselves, but from compilations of them, made about the fourteenth century. ## INSCRIPTIONS AT NEW-GRANGE.

The moſt ancient inſcriptions now remaining in Ireland, if not in theſe parts of Europe, are undoubtedly thoſe found in the tumulus or mount of New-Grange near Drogheda in the county of Meath. ->No. 3,<-

Is found on the front of the covering stone of the
east tabernacle, and is written in symbolic cha-
racters, signifying the *House of God*. It is remark-
able that all the ancient altars found in Ireland, and
now distinguished by the name of Cromleachs or
sloping stones, were originally called *Bothal* or the
House of God; and they seem to be of the same
species as those mentioned in the book of *Genesis*,
called by the Hebrews *Bethel*, which has the same
signification as the Irish *Bothal*. The tabernacles
in the mount of New-Grange have an exact con-
formity to the Cromleachs, found in different parts
of the kingdom.

->No. 4,<-

Is found on the south side of the east tabernacle,
written in the Ogham and symbolic characters.
The symbol is that representing the earth and
universal nature, and with the Ogham which is
written from the left to the right, makes *a mor an*
*Ops*, that is, *to the great mother Ops*, or to the great
mother Nature.

->No. 5,<-

Is found on the front stone of the north tabernacle;
and represents chance, fate or providence.

->No. 6,<-

Is found on the north stone of the west tabernacle, written in the Ogham, Bobeloth and Ogham Croabh characters, from the left to the right ; the first character being an Ogham Œ, the second a Bobeloth M, and the others in the Ogham Croabh are G, U, H, making *Oenguh, Oemguth,* that is, the sepulchre of the hero *(m)*.

->No. 7,<-

Is found on a stone on the left of the gallery, is written in the Ogham, from right to left, terminating in the *Cionn fa eite*, being a *fur, daim, siuc*, that is, men, oxen, swine; probably specifying the several species of victims sacrificed at this temple, in honour of universal nature, providence and the manes of the hero interred within, and to whom the three tabernacles appear to have been dedicated, and which were the principal objects of worship among all the Celtic tribes.

At what time this tumulus was erected cannot be ascertained ; it probably was not long before the art of writing became universal in the island, as all the different species are contained in the inscriptions ; if it was not erected by the founder of the convention of Taragh himself, as a temple and sepulchre for his family, towards the close of the second century ; it was however constantly distinguished by the name of *Oenguh* or *Oengus*, viz. the tomb of the chiefs or heroes, by the body of the people ; and we find it mentioned in the Chronicon Scotorum,

*(m) Oem* or *oen* signifies a hollow or dome, figuratively a tomb or sepulchre, and *gub* or *guth* a commander or chief.

torum, with the grove which surrounded it, by the name of *Fiodh Aongusa*, or the grove of Aongus, or rather the grove of the sepulchre of the heroes ; though several persons have imagined, that a chief of the name of Aongus or Oengus was interred here.

Aongus or Oengus was the name of the district adjacent to this monument, and which was also called *Magh-Breaffail* or the plain of the noble shades ; the chiefs of which, as customary among the ancient Irish, took the name of Aongus from their district, which in process of time became a family and hereditary name.

Inscriptions, as curious as those of New-Grange, are found on two stone crosses, in the church-yard of Castle-dermot in the county of Kildare. These inscriptions are written in the *Bobeloth*, *Bethluisnon*, *Ogham*, *Ogham Croabh* and *Symbolic characters*, mixed.

The characters on theſe croſſes are all in creux, and from two to four inches in length, though now ſo much worn by time, that the true form of ſeveral can with difficulty be traced ; they appear to have ſupplied the place of an image, and probably at the time of their erection were not underſtood by the people, but were intended as *Abraxas* or *Chaldaic ſigna*, which contained ſome hidden myſtery, and which the devotees eſteemed efficacious either in the remiſſion of their ſins or in the cure of ſome bodily infirmity. The Saxons and Germans uſed for this purpoſe the ancient *Runic*, which on the introduction of the Latin had become obſolete, and therefore not underſtood by the people. To ſuch a degree of infatuation were the people arrived for charms and taliſmans in the ninth and tenth centuries, that the *Runic* letters in which they were generally written, were in a council held at *Toledo* in 1115, forbid to be uſed ; and the Germans laid them aſide in 1001, by the perſuaſion of the pope and of *Sifrid* a Britiſh biſhop (n). <language>English</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>

<header>DRUIDISM REVIVED.</header>

which the characters on these crosses are placed, was not peculiar to the ancient Irish, but appears to be the general method used by all the Christian clergy during the middle ages, in their inscriptions and talismans, probably to render them more inexplicable; for several inscriptions have been found at Constantinople, written in this manner, in the Greek letters intermixed with the Chaldaic signa, resembling in several instances the characters on the crosses at Castle-dermot (*o*). As some of these inscriptions are evidently of the tenth century, we may reasonably conclude those on the crosses are not much older; indeed every part of the building, especially the tower and ornaments, show them to be of that period.

From these crosses we may observe, that the Bobeloth characters and several of the druidic symbols were not intirely lost in the tenth and eleventh centuries, though it is probable that the clergy had long neglected to use them in their writings; they appear however to have been retained in the minds of the people, which they mixed with the Latin characters in their public inscriptions down to the fifteenth century. And the ancient pagan Saxon characters are yet, in a great measure, retained by the common people of England, which they use as brands and marks for the parishes and hundreds, though their power and signification have long since been lost.

---

(*o*) Vide Dissert. Imp. Constantinopolitanorum, seu de inferioris ævi vel imperii, uti vocant, Numismatibus. Dufresne. gloss. tom. 3.

### OF THE
# ORIGIN AND LANGUAGE
### OF THE
# IRISH,
#### AND OF THE,
## LEARNING
#### OF THE
## DRUIDS.

To develope from obscurity the primeval colonization of Europe is an arduous undertaking. Imperfect hints and mutilated records are suspicious guides in the wide ocean of remote times; and yet even these afford some clue to the sagacious inquirer, and no improbable conjectures have been formed on this subject. In the opinion of some learned men, Europe received its first colonies from three distinct bodies of emigrants, that is, the inhabitants of the west and south from one, those of the east from another, and those of the north and midland parts from a third. From whence we may reasonably infer, that ancient Europe received its inhabitants after the universal deluge, like most other countries, at different periods and from different races of men; as is conformable to the

<vocab>Irish, Druids, Europe, colonization, universal deluge</vocab>

--- Page 243 ---
<language>English</language>
<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>219</page-num>
<header>ORIGIN AND LANGUAGE, &c.</header>

testimony of most of the ancients; who constantly considered the universal inhabitants of the several countries of uncultivated Europe as of three distinct races, that is, the Celtæ, the Sarmatæ, and the Scythæ.

The Celtæ, from sacred as well as prophane writers, appear to have been the first of the human race who replenished with inhabitants the wilds of Europe, after the destruction of the old world by water. They were frequently called by the Greeks and Romans, Calts, Gauls, Gallatæ, Celtæ and Cimbri; according to the different dialects of the Celtic or Gomerian tongue spoken by these people, who originally inhabited or rather perambulated all the countries of ancient Europe, from Pontus Euxinus to the Chersonesus, and from the Vistula to the pillars of Hercules; comprehending the present Germany, Poland, Hungary, Italy, Spain, Portugal, France and the British isles. They generally distinguished themselves by the name of Calt, Cuilt and Caël, that is woodlanders, from inhabiting woods and forests; for Cale and Chille, in the Gomerian tongue signify a wood, and from thence undoubtedly is derived the Latin *Celta* and the Greek *Keltoi*; names, which have ever distinguished the aboriginal inhabitants of Europe among the ancients.

The second colony which contributed to the population of ancient Europe, appear to be the Sarmatæ; who were apparently descended from the ancient inhabitants of Persia, Media and those countries now appertaining to Asia-minor, and lying between the Euxine and Caspian sea, the ancient

<meta>catchword: Phrygia,</meta>

<header>ORIGIN AND LANGUAGE OF THE IRISH,</header>

Phrygia, Armenia and Iberia. These people were called by the Greeks, Phœnicians and Hebrews, Sar-madæ, that is, descendants of the Medes. They probably made their first establishment in Europe on their revolt from the Assyrians, about 746 years before the Christian era, where in process of time, they inhabited that tract of country comprehending the present Hungary, Bohemia, Poland and the greatest part of Turkey, the ancient *Sarmatia Europea*.

The third European colony was the Scythæ, a people descended from the Scythæ of Asia; who in former ages, inhabited all the country at present distinguished by Great Tartary and Russia, the ancient *Scythia Asiatica*. They were called Scythæ by the Greeks, from their unsettled mode of life, and are supposed to have made their way into Europe either round the gulphs of Finland and Bothnia into the ancient Scandinavia, from whence, in process of time, they overflowed the middle regions by Jutland and the Danish isles, or across the Vistula by the southern coasts of the Baltic (*p*).

From these three people who were seperate and distinct races, and as different in their language, religion, manners and customs as a barbarous state, (common to all) could admit, not only ancient but modern Europe is indebted for its inhabitants; for from the Celtæ are descended the greater part of the present inhabitants of Ireland, Wales and the western parts of Scotland, with the body of the

present French, Spaniards and Italians, as also numbers of the Swiss and Germans. From the Sarmatæ are descended the greater part of the inhabitants of Bóhemia, Hungary, Bucharia, Sclavonia, Poland and the greater part of Turkey ; and from the Scythæ are descended the Swedes, Danes, Germans and English, with the eastern Scotch and numbers of the Russians, also several of the French, Swiss, Spaniards and Italians ; from the irruptions of the Goths, Vandals and Franks in the third and fourth centuries, who were different tribes of those people.

At what time the Celtes, as the aboriginal inhabitants, had planted colonies in the several European countries, and from thence crossed the sea to the British isles, we have no certain information. It is certain from the most ancient and authentic Irish historians, as Cormac and Tighernach, who make not the least mention of those fables, (which during the latter ages have disgraced the Hibernian historic page) that the ancient inhabitants of this island derived their origin from those of Britain. The time therefore, in which Britain received its original inhabitants will, in some measure, determine that of Ireland. The Celtic tribes who, in a very early period, rather perambulated than inhabited the wilds of ancient Europe, were probably neither strong nor numerous ; but wandered from place to place, as the convenience of pasturage for their flocks, hunting and other circumstances might admit, and therefore cannot be supposed to have committed themselves to the hazards of the sea in search of new habitations, until obliged thereto by

<header>ORIGIN AND LANGUAGE OF THE IRISH,</header>
<meta>catchword: As</meta>

birthright, making them a subsequent colony to the Fir Bolgæ. The Fir Bolgæ, so much spoken of by the ancient Irish historians, appear to have been of the second migration from Britain, and descendants of the ancient Silures, who inhabited the country on the north and south sides of the Severn, and who, on the arrival of the Belgæ under Divitiacus retired into Ireland, and established a colony on the south and east sides of the Shannon mouth, about eighty years before the Christian era, as is particularly mentioned by Ossian ($t$), who says, the Bolgæ under the conduct of Lathmon chief of Lumon ($u$), came from Cluba or the crooked bay, in Innis-hona an island beyond the waves, and settled in Culbin or the lesser crooked bay ; these people do not appear however to have distinguished themselves by the name of Bolgæ, but of Momonii or children of the wave, from coming over sea; and Momoniensis or Mumhan the southern part of Ireland, has been ever thus denominated by the ancient Irish writers.

Thus were the north and south parts of Ireland peopled by two grand migrations from Britain, and the other parts also received from that island subsequent colonies, who fled from the terror of the Roman arms ; for Tacitus observes, that in the time of Augustus, migrations from Britain to Ireland were frequent ; and we may add, in much later periods, especially on the arrival of the Saxons in the fifth century. Whence we may infer, the entire population of this country from Britain was completed in the space of 800 years.

it is evident from the assertions of Strabo, Dyonisius, Caesar, Tacitus and Pliny, that a considerable commerce was carried on with Ireland and Britain by the Punic, Iberian and Gallic merchants, from the first century antecedent to the Christian era, to the close of the second subsequent to it. It is sincerely to be wished however, that some of the universities of Britain or Ireland, would encourage the study of the Irish or Erse language, even in this late period, as several subjects might by that means be explained, which appear now inexplicable.

From a neglect of the cultivation of the Celtic tongue, with the several characters in which it was anciently written, all knowledge of the arts and sciences, cultivated by our heathen ancestors, has been intirely lost; the only fragments now remaining of them lie scattered in the works of the Greek and Roman writers; some few excepted, which have been transmitted by tradition. Therefore to see this subject treated here in a circumstantial manner, cannot be expected; nor indeed is it possible, from the few lights relative thereto which we are able to obtain.

We have observed that all knowledge among the ancient inhabitants of these isles was confined to a class of men called druids. These people, whom we may consider as the body of the learned, were of different orders; to each of which, the cultivation of a particular art and science was appropriated; and as the whole class was held in the most honourable estimation, none but those of noble parentage could be initiated into their mysteries; all the Celtic tribes in general, after the manner of the ancient

<header>ORIGIN AND LANGUAGE OF THE IRISH,</header>

Greeks, esteeming it ignoble to instruct any of the plebeian orders in the liberal arts and sciences (b).

The druidic orders consisted of two principal classes, that is, the *sacred* and *prophane*. The prophane or lowest order was denominated *bhardagh* or *bardos*, that is, learned men (c); to this class appertained the study of oratory, history, laws, poetry and music (d). For instructing youth in those sciences, schools were established in groves and caves in different parts of the island, as is agreeable to the assertions of the Irish antiquaries (e). One of these academies is mentioned by Ossian to be in Ulster, others were at Clogher, Ardmagh, Taragh, &c. and in general all the celebrated schools, established in Ireland by the Christian clergy in the fifth century, were erected on the ruins of the druidic academies. The course in these seminaries, besides the constant use of arms, was 1st oratory, 2d music, 3d poetry, and 4th history (f); in each of these, as they advanced, the students took their degrees according to the bent of their studies; those who professed only music, obtained the name of *citharadagh* or *clarsacha*, (g) those who professed historic poetry and music obtained the title of *bhard*; and those who studied only poetry, containing their laws, obtained the title of *brehons* or judges. denominated *trudhii* or *turduli*, that is, diviners and interpreters of the Gods (*m*). Their studies were confined to theology and the sublime sciences, and consisted like the *bhards* of several degrees or orders; that is, the *drudhicydeigh*, the *drudhibhaitheigh*, the *drudhicerglios* and the *samodhii*.

The *drudhicydeigh* (*n*) or the interpreters of the Gods of the forests, resided in the sacred groves in caves, or in the trunk of an hollow oak; they divined by the motion of the leaves of trees, by the blowing of the wind, and by long square slips of wood taken from several trees. Their particular studies were botany and physic.

The *drudhibhaitheigh* (*o*), or as they were called by the Latin writers, *vates* and *ubates*, were the sacrificers; and divined by the entrails and flowing of the blood of the victims at the time of sacrifice (*p*).

The *drudhicerglios* (*q*) presided over the manes and tombs of heroes, they were the dreamers, and divined by dreams and visions of the night (*r*).

The *samodhii* or *samothæi*, that is, the wisdom of the gods, were of the highest degree of the druidic order; they cultivated the study of theology, astronomy, and moral and natural philosophy, and divined by the aspect of the sun, moon and stars,

No person could be admitted into the druidic

pupils of the druids was not peculiar to them, the
ancient Greeks had the same, for we find *Hippo-*
*crates* swore his pupils on being admitted under his
tuition (*u*).

<header>ORIGIN AND LANGUAGE OF THE IRISH,</header>

markable for their strength and gracefulness of person; wherefore, when two competitors arose whose mental and corporeal accomplishments were nearly equal, the decision was left to the fate of arms, by single combat (*w*). The time necessary to obtain the several degrees in the schools of the bards was ten or twelve years, and in those of the druids nearly as long; whence, between twenty and thirty years close application was required to obtain the degree of a <term>samothei</term> (*x*).

In speaking of the several species of learning cultivated by these heathen philosophers, we shall only mention here the secular, that is, oratory, poetry, music, physic, cosmography, astronomy and ethics, reserving the theological to be spoken of more fully hereafter. To speak with ease and eloquence in public assemblies, was esteemed the greatest ornament in the circle of druidic literature, and as this was the most effectual method of laying a true foundation for poetic and musical composition, no pains were omitted to ground the young pupils in oratory and elocution, on their entrance into the academies. To find a barbarous and uncivilized nation, cultivating with assiduity, a branch of literature seldom attained in perfection by the most refined and polished societies, may at first appear somewhat extraordinary; but we ought to consider, that true eloquence is not confined to any particular state of society. The harangues of an Indian <term>sachem</term> at the head of his tribe, has often more energy than is to be found in the most learned assemblies;

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

assemblies; and the orations of Demosthenes are more to be admired than those delivered in a more improved state of the Grecian empire. In the early stages of society the passions alone are consulted, in the later the reason. Man living in uncultivated deserts, and supported by the chace, has few abstract ideas; reasoning therefore, from a long train of connected subjects would be lost on him, he would neither have patience to attend to the conclusion nor understand the argument. Whence the druidic oratory was intirely calculated to work on the passions, consisting of energetic expressions and strong metaphors, as is evinced through every species of their poetic compositions.

To judge of the Celtic poetry by the few remains to be found at this time in Ireland, would be improper; none of the compositions of this kind appear older than the fourteenth century; some of them indeed are taken from much earlier productions, but so mutilated by the later bards, as to have little resemblance to the originals. The only genuine remains of the old druidic poetry are in the works of Ossian, to be found in the highlands of Scotland; true and elegant translations of the greater part of the productions of this noble heathen bard, who flourished about the close of the third century, have been given to the public some years since, by Mr. M'Pherson. From these poems it is apparent, that the Celtic poetry consisted of several species, as the elegiac, the lyric, heroic, epic and dramatic, as has been constantly asserted by the Irish antiquaries and several of the ancients (y).

<header>ORIGIN AND LANGUAGE OF THE IRISH,</header>

The elegiac was intirely confined to funeral obsequies and other serious subjects.

The lyric contained their love sonnets, pastoral pieces, &c.

The heroic, under which species we may comprehend the epic and in some instances the dramatic, contained the poems relative to their history and actions of their chiefs; beautiful specimens of this composition are given in the works of Ossian; they were performed generally at the feasts of the nobles, assemblies of the state, on the eve of battle, the obtaining of victory, and indeed on every other public occasion (z); their performance, when circumstances admitted, was grand and noble; the chiefs being seated in the open air during the night, with torch light, in a circle, on mounds of turf or skins of wild beasts; the bards standing in the centre, recited the narrative part, in a kind of recitative accompanied by the harp; after which, the lyric part was sung in full chorus, after the manner of the Greeks, in which were frequently introduced symphonies of pure instrumental music by the <term>clarsacha</term>, standing on the outer circumference of the circle (a); so that perhaps there was not a more august and noble spectacle, than to hear the recital of an elegant historic production, at the general assembly of the states, when the most eminent bards throughout the realm were collected; there being the greatest probability that they far surpassed, in noble sentiment, beautiful expression and true melody,

---

(z) Amm. Marcell. l. 17. c. 13. p. 146. Diodor. Sicul. l. 5. 212. Liv. 42. 60. and the Poems of Ossian.
(a) Poems of Ossian.

melody, all the modern compositions of operas and oratorios, especially after the establishment of the convention of Taragh. To that celebrated institution, which probably was erected in imitation of those of the ancient Iberians, mentioned by *Strabo*, (*b*) the Celtic poetry in these islands seems to have been indebted, for that elegance and refinement which we find in the works of *Ossian*. For about the middle of the third century, as appears from *Ossian* and *Hector Boethius*, *Fingall* or *Fynnan*, called by the Irish *Fin mac Comhal* and great grandson of *Connor mor*, instituted a like convention at *Selma* in *Scotland* (*c*); so that the poems of *Ossian* may be considered as the most correct specimens of the Celtic poetry, being composed in the most learned and refined period of antiquity. After the establishment of Christianity, and the druidic order was neglected, their poetry suffered considerable diminutions, especially the historic, though the lyric retained its perfection several centuries after, and some compositions of that species are still to be found in Ireland and in the highlands of *Scotland*, excellent in their kind.

As all, or most of the Celtic poetry was set to music, the Irish antiquaries have said much relative to their ancient musical composition; but how much it exceeded, or came short of the modern, cannot perhaps be determined, it not being certain, that any of the druidic music has been handed down to us. The national music, found at this day both in Ireland and the highlands of *Scotland*, has great

Whether the druidic music resembled any of these is <unclear>not</unclear> certain ; there is found in some of the remote parts of the isles of Scotland, music of a noble simple nature, exceedingly expressive, and bearing evident marks of great antiquity ; it is said to be some of the music to which the poems of Ossian were originally set, if so, the Hibernian and British druids cultivated music with the same success they did poetry ; some also of the Irish airs appear to be very old ; and if they are not some of the remains, are at least in imitation of their ancient music. We must not expect however, that the Hibernian Celtic music contained pieces in the various parts of harmonic composition ; its merit, like that of the ancient Greeks, depended intirely on melody, and even in this, of no great latitude ; the scale exceeding little more than a single octave in the diatonic, the chromatic was entirely unknown. This defect however in the druidic musical scale did not prevent their having pieces in the several species of melodious composition ; as the penseroso, allegro, martial, &c. The penseroso, called by them *geantraidheacht* (d) or sorrowful, was used in the requiem of the dead, and on other solemn occasions (e). The allegro called *langotraidheacht* or delightful was used in their dances, and generally adapted to their lyric compositions. The *amoroso*,

species of wind instruments, called *stuic* and *adharcaidh ciuil*; *stuic* signifies a tube or pipe, and was probably the common pipe; *adharcaidh ciuil* signifies a collection of pipes joined together, and appears to be no other than the bag-pipes, so much used in Ireland at present ; as neither of these instruments seem to have been known in this island in the days of Ossian, they probably were introduced by the foreign merchants about the fourth or fifth century, and seem to be of Gallic or Iberian origin, and to be those mentioned by the Latin writers, under the denomination of organs (g). As to the trumpet and drum, mentioned by Cambrensis, they were of Scythic origin, and introduced by the Danes.

Poetry and music appear to have been the sciences, cultivated with the greatest success by the -druids; though their knowledge in cosmography and astronomy was not despicable, considering their mode of life, and their total want of instruments proper to make experiments and observations. Their ideas relative to the origin of things were nearly the same as those of the Egyptian priests and Persian magi; they maintained that the world was eternal, and engendered by fire, which they considered the active principle of nature (h); that the principle opposite to fire, and constantly at variance with it, was water; which two principles, after contending together for some time, would alternately succeed, first water and then fire; that during the dominion

tions, especially those of the northern hemisphere ; but how far they succeeded in this, it is not possible to determine, though some of their names are mentioned by Ossian.

In their chronology, called by them *chronog* (o), they calculated time by the night, beginning at sunset, according to the general practice of antiquity ; their seasons were generally regulated by the moon, after the manner of the Egyptian priests, and their years by the sun, whence the ancient Irish for a year is *bealaine* (p).

In mathematical knowledge they seem to have been extremely defective, it not being certain what method they had of numerating and performing arithmetical calculations. They appear to have been acquainted with some geometrical figures, as the circle, triangle, square, and polygon (q), but the external form of these bodies, probably terminated their geometrical knowledge ; indeed living in an uncultivated country, and leading an unsettled life, they were not under the necessity of cultivating geometry like the Egyptians. In anatomy, they appear to have had a superficial knowledge of the muscles, veins and nerves, as they frequently divined by them in their sacrifices (r). In surgery they generally applied herbs to wounds and fractures ; indeed vegetables composed the whole of their *materia medica*, and they applied them in all physical cases, both internal and external,

though the generality of diseases were attempted to be cured by charms and incantations.

Their morality consisted of short sentences or proverbs, which they obliged the people to retain in their memories ; the principal of which were, to fear the gods, do no ill, and study to be valiant (s).

But the science to which the druids paid the greatest attention was that of divination, to be perfect master of which, was thought to be unattainable by any one person ; wherefore it was divided into classes, that each druid might apply to the cultivation of some particular branch, whence the several orders of the druids were denominated from the species of divination they professed.

The sublime parts of their philosophy and theology were first taught their pupils in the schools of the bards under fiction and allegory (t), after the manner of the orientals and all remote nations of antiquity, but were not explained until their admission into the druid order.

To this concise account of the druidic learning, it may not be improper to mention the system of education given by them to the people ; reserving a more circumstantial explanation of their erudition, till we fully treat of the religion, poetry, music, architecture, army, navy, customs and manners of the ancient pagan Irish, under distinct heads.

The Celtic nations have ever been looked on by the Greeks and Romans as an ignorant and barbarous people; the lower orders undoubtedly were so, but this certainly was not the case with the nobless.

<header>ORIGIN AND LANGUAGE OF THE IRISH,</header>

There was perhaps no nation of antiquity, where the education of the young nobility, was so much attended to as among the ancient Irish ; they were not only initiated early into the use of arms, but constantly went through a regular course of oratory, history, poetry and music, in the academies of the bards ; from whence, if they thought proper, they were admitted into the druidic order, and initiated into all their mystic rites ; for which reason we find that several of the ancient Irish kings were not only bards but druids. Even the fair sex were not neglected, and the ancient Hibernian ladies received an education, according to their mode of life, equal, if not superior, to that of the moderns. The young ladies in the early ages, so far from being put under the care of foreign tutoresses collected from the lower people, without education, sentiment and often without principle, were committed to the care of druids, who paid constant attention to their mental and corporeal accomplishments (u) ; whilst music, eloquence and poetry embellished their minds, the exercise of the chace, archery and throwing the lance, served to give their bodies health, vigour and beauty, the constant characteristics of the Celtic ladies ; even the line did not terminate here, those who attained to perfection the learning of the bards, on application, were admitted into the druidic order (w), and initiated into all the sublime tenets of their religion and philosophy, where they became the priestesses in several modes of their worship,

worship, and were often chosen in preference to
the druïds themselves, in drawing presages from

On the establishment of the Christian religion,
and the druidic order being abolished, the Hiber-
nian system of education as well as learning suffered
considerable alterations. For the several sciences
being clothed in a foreign language, few, except
those intended for the priesthood, would be at the
trouble of cultivating knowledge of such difficult
access; especially, as it was different from that
they had been accustomed to. In consequence, the
education of the laity, and even the nobless, were
not much attended to; and after the arrival of the
English, the wars attending the constant struggle
for liberty, for near 400 years, so far perverted
the mind from literary pursuits, that in the fifteenth
century, few of the Irish nobility, could either
read or write (y).

# Advertiſement.

**THE** Eſſay on the **ANTIQUITY** of the **IRISH LANGUAGE** publiſhed in the Year 1772 being out of print, and much inquired after, the Author beſtowed part of his leiſure in correcting and making additions to it ; but being called upon to attend the ſervice of his country at this critical period, he left his papers in the hands of a friend to diſpoſe of as he ſhould think proper. On conſulting ſome learned and judicious friends, they agreed that the Eſſay thus reviſed and improved would be a moſt acceptable preſent to the curious ; in compliance with this determination, the Editor now preſents it to the Public as the **EIGHTH NUMBER** of the **COLLECTANEA DE REBUS HIBERNICIS**, hoping that the unavoidable abſence of the Author will be admitted as an excuſe for any errors that may appear in it.

# P R E F A C E.

IRELAND, properly ſo called, was probably the firſt of the Britiſh iſles that got the Name of Thule, as being the firſt the Carthaginians met with ſteering their courſe northward, when they departed from Cape Fineſtre the northern head-land of Spain. And this iſland ſeems to be the ſame ſaid by Ariſtotle to have been diſcovered by the Carthaginians, Lib. de mirabil. auſcultat. where he ſays, “ extra columnas Herculis aiunt in mari a Carthaginienſibus inſulam fertilem inventam, ut quæ tam ſylvarum copia, quam fluminibus navigationi idoneis abundet, cum reliquis fructibus floreat vehementer, diſtans a continente plurimum dierum itinere, &c.”

Bochart confirms this by what he obſerves that the ancient writer Antonius Diogenes (who wrote twenty-four books of the ſtrange things related of Thule, not long after the time of Alexander the Great) had his hiſtory from certain tables of cypreſs wood digged at Tyrus out of the tombs of Mantima and Dercelis, who had gone from Tyrus to Thule, and had remained ſome time there.

The ſituation of Thule has been much controverted; yet all agree it was ſome place towards the north, with reſpect to the firſt diſcoverers, and

<language>English</language>
<page-type>preface</page-type>
<header>P R E F A C E .</header>

many make it to be one of the British isles. This agrees perfectly with the situation of Ireland, for the Carthaginians in sailing from Cadiz having once cleared Cape St. Vincent, had Ireland in a direct northern course before them.

<margin>(a) Camd. Br. p. 1407.</margin>
The ancients seem mostly to agree, that Thule was one of those islands that are called British. Strabo, one of the most ancient and best geographers extant, speaks thus ; Pytheas Massiliensis says, it is about Thule, the furthest north of all the British isles. Yet he himself maketh it nearer than Pytheas did : But I think, says he, that northern bound to be much nearer to the south; for they who survey that part of the globe, can give no account beyond Ireland, an isle which lies not far towards the north, before Britain; inhabited by wild people almost starved with cold ; there, therefore, I am of opinion the utmost bound is to be placed ; so that in his opinion, that which he calls Ireland must be Thule (a).

Catullus is of the same mind.

> Sive trans altas
> Graditur Alpes,
> Cæsaris visens
> Monumenta magni,
> Gallicum Rhenum,
> Horribilesque et
> Ultimos Britannos.

> Whether he o'er the Alps his way pursue
> The mighty Cæsar's monuments to view,
> As Gallic Rhine and Britons that excel
> In fierceness, who on the earth's limits dwell.

Bound to the world's remotest Briton's shore.

->*Cærulus haud aliter cum dimicat incola Thules,*<-
->*Agmina falcifero circumvenit acta covina.*<-
->**SILIUS ITALICUS.**<-

As <term>Thule</term>’s blue inhabitants surround
Their foes with chariots hook’d; and them confound.

Pliny places <term>Thulè</term> among the British isles, and Tacitus **(c)** says, when the Roman navy sailed about Britain, *despecta est et Thule*, “they saw <term>Thule</term> also.”

Statius ad Claud. Uxorem, describes <term>Thule</term> to the westward of Britain.

—— *et se gelidas irem mansuras ad Arctas,*
*Vel super Hesperiæ vada caligantia Thules.*

If in the cold north I go to abide,
Or on dark seas which western <term>Thule</term> hide.

Although the Romans never were in Ireland, yet Statius, with the liberty of a poet, has certainly brought them there in this verse, apparently for the honour of having them in <term>Thule</term>.

—— *tu disce patrem, quantusque nigrantem*
*Fluctibus occiduis, fessoque Hyperione Thulen*
*Intrarit, mandata gerens.*

Learn, from thy sight, how glorious he was,
When he did with the senate’s order pass

> O'er to dark Thule, in that ocean, west,
> Where Phœbus gives his weary horses rest (d).

Qu. Where could he conduct them westward from Britain, but to Thule—to Ireland.

Sir R. Sibbald explains the transmarinæ Gentes or Scotorum a Circio, i. e. the Scots from the north-west and beyond the seas, mentioned by Bede, to be Scots and Pights, because, says he, Ireland cannot be said to lie to the north-west of the Roman province. I do affirm the Scoti or northern Irish, from whom all expeditions passed into Albion, lie due north-west of the Roman province.

Ireland was ever antiently remarkable for learning, it was the insula sanctorum. Stephanus Byzantinus says, ἹΕΡΝΗ, νῆσος ἐν τῷ πέρατι, πρὸς δυσμαῖς. Upon which words Holstenius thus remarks, *Ἱέρνη illa insula est, quæ hodie Hibernia dicitur.* Aristoteles de Mundo : Ἐν τῷ ὠκεανῷ γε μὴν νῆσοι μέγισταί τε τυγχάνουσι οὖσαι δύο, Βρετανικαὶ λεγόμεναι, Ἄλβιον καὶ Ἱέρνη. *In Oceano insulæ duæ sitæ sunt, quam maxime, quas Britannicas apellant, Albion et Ierna* : de hac vide plur. apud Andr. Schottum lib. II. Observat. cap. 20. Festo Avieno in ora maritima Hibernia vocatur *sacra insula*. Quod quam aliam ob causam fecerit nunc non succurrit, nisi quod * ἱερὴ legerit pro Ἱέρνη. Feſtus Avienus lived in the fourth century, therefore this was not named the holy iſland after St. Patrick's converſion, as ſome think, for he did not arrive here till the beginning of the fifth century; this muſt therefore be the iſland ſacred to Apollo (that is to Baal) of which Diodorus Siculus makes particular mention. <margin>(f) Specimen Iſland. hiſt. p. 2. p. 120.</margin>
Thus, Arngrimus Jonas deſcribes Thule (*f*):

> —— penetravit ad Indos,
> Ingeniumque potens ultima Thule colit.
> His eloquence did reach the utmoſt Indies,
> And powerful wit enlightened fartheſt Thule.

And then he adds; from whence it may fairly be inferred, that either Britain or (as Pliny will have it) ſome iſland of Britain was the ultima Thule; yet Sibbald will interpret *ſome iſland of Britain* to be Britain itſelf.

Again, "In the hiſtory of the kings of Norway, it is ſaid that king Magnus, in an expedition to the Orcades, Hebrides, Scotland and Britain, touched alſo at the iſland of Thule and ſubdued it." Here Scotland, Britain and Thule are very plainly diſtinguiſhed.

Wernerus Ralwingus ſays, in the time of pope Linus aroſe the Scottiſh nation of Picts and Hibernians in Albion, which is a part of England; that is, a nation of Picts and Hibernians aroſe in Albion a part of England. As plain and intelligible as this is, Sibbald will have Hibernia to be part of Scotland.

Strabo always mentions Thule and Britain as the Britiſh iſles. Speaking of Pytheas's blunders, he

Hinc illius Africo vento exurgente post immensa pericula in *Tyle* vel Thule ultimam detorquentur.

Some derive the name Thule from the Arabic word *Tule*, which signifies afar off, and think it was in allusion to this the poets usually called it *ultima Thule*. Bochart derives it from a Phoenician word signifying darkness. But the words *Thual* and *Thuathal* in the Irish and probably in the Punic language signified the north, as also the left hand, agreeable to the oriental manner of naming the cardinal points with respect to their looking towards the east in their devotions. Thus the north part of Munster, in old manuscripts is called *Thuathal-Mhumhan* or *Thuath-Mhumhan*, in English

So also the northern province of Ireland retains the word *Thual* to this day, in *Coige Thualle* & corruptè *Coige Ulla* (the *th* being an hiatus) in English *Ulster*. To what I have already said I will adjoin the opinion of a gentleman who has made many curious researches into the antiquities of Great Britain. "The Thule of the ancients seems most clearly to have been Ireland, from the manner in which Statius addresses a poem to Crispinus, whose father had carried the emperor's commands to Thule.

> ——tu disce patrem, quantusque nigrantem
> Fluctibus occiduis, fessoque *Hyperione* Thulen
> Intravit mandata gerens.

It should also seem, from other parts of the same poem, that this general had crossed from Scotland to the north of Ireland or Thule :

> Quod si te magno tellus *frænata* parenti
> Accipiat, quantum ferus exultabit Araxes ?
> Quanta Caledonios attollet gloria campos ?
> Cum tibi longævus referet trucis incola terræ,
> Hic suetus dare jura parens, hoc cespite turmas
> Affari ; nitidas speculas, castellaque longé.
> Aspicis ? ille dedit cinxitque hæc mænia fossâ.

->STATIUS, v. 14.<-

Although Ireland be the first Thule discovered
by the Carthaginians, says Sir Robert Sibbald,
yet it is not that Thule in which the Romans were
and made conquest of; for it is certain they never
were in Ireland, properly so called. The *Horesti*,
that is the Highlanders were called *Hyberni*, says he,
as being a colony from Ireland. Yet Strabo says,
*Qui Iernen Britanniam viderunt, nihil de Thule*
*dicunt* ($i$). But seeing Scotland has those within
herself who are able to trace her original from the
highest antiquity, I will only point out the fountain
from whence I can conceive these truths are to be
drawn, and offer some things which I would have
them diligently to consider; for in this point I
profess myself a sceptick.

First therefore of their original, and then of the

In another place,
> *Scotorum cumulos flevit glacialis Iberne.* *
> And frozen Ireland moan'd the crowding heaps
> Of murthered Scots (*k*).

The first inhabitants of Ireland came from Britain. Ireland was inhabited by Scots. Paulus Orosius. lib. 1. cap. 2. He is an author of the fifth century.

Gildas who must have perfectly known that country, assures us, that in the 6th century the Picts and the Scots inhabited Ireland. Basnage Hist. Eccles. (*l*). This testimony of Gildas is confirmed in our antient topography.

It was a received opinion in the time of Propertius, who lived under Augustus Cæsar, that the Irish were descended from the Scythians, witness that verse, lib. 4. el. 3.
> 'Hibernique Getæ, pictoque Britannia curru.

Whence it appears that the Irish were descended from the Getæ (Goths) a branch of the Scythians, the common origin of all the Celtic tribes who inhabited Europe.

*Scytæ in quarta ætate mundi obtinuerint Hiberniam*, says Usher (*m*).

*Britones in tertia mundi ætate in Britanniam, Scotti in quarta venerunt in Hiberniam.* Huntingdon, lib. 1.

Hence it appears that the Scoti were a colony of the Scytæ ; that they were the same people, and even preserved and bore the same name with the alteration of one letter only, the *o* for the *y*, owing

*Diodorus Siculus* (n) ſuppoſes, as a thing known and out of diſpute, that the inhabitants of *Ireland* were *Britons*, and conſequently deſcended from the *Gauls*, *Galatæ*, *Skeltæ* or *Celts*.

*Buchanan* (o) confirms the *Iriſh* hiſtory, that numbers of *Spaniards* fled to *Ireland*, being much diſquieted in their own country by the *Carthaginians* and *Romans*, and that all the north ſide of *Spain* was poſſeſſed by *Gallic* colonies. He contradicts *Tacitus*, who ſays, the weſt ſide of *Albium* was poſſeſſed immediately by *Spaniards*, but that they came from *Ireland*; for, ſays he, all our annals relate that the *Scots* paſſed more than once out of *Ireland* into *Albium*; firſt of all under *Ferguſius* ſon of *Ferchard*. And *Bede*'s account of the *Scythians* coming to *Ireland* by diſtreſs of weather correſponds with our *Iriſh* hiſtory.
